prompt: A regional insurer receives about 2,000 first-notice-of-loss emails a day. For each one the team wants to extract the policy number, loss date and loss type, look the policy up in the claims system, and file a structured claim record. The steps are the same for every email and the business wants per-step audit logs. Which architecture fits best?

options.text: A fixed workflow of sequenced model calls, with the lookup done in code between steps
An autonomous agent that reads each email and plans its own tool calls for every request
An orchestrator model that spawns one specialist agent per field and merges their outputs
A single prompt holding the email, the claims schema and the entire policy register

explanation: Correct: A. The steps are fully known in advance and never branch, so a fixed workflow gives predictable behaviour, a log line per step and a cheap place to validate between steps. Why not the others: B spends tokens planning a path that is already known; C adds multi-agent coordination to an extraction one call handles; D stuffs the whole register into every call and cannot be audited by step.

prompt: A law firm wants an assistant that answers partners' questions about ongoing matters. Some questions need one document lookup, others need a dozen searches across filings, a date calculation and a draft memo, and the path is only clear once early results come back. Which pattern should the architect start from?

options.text: A routing workflow that classifies each question and sends it to one of four pipelines
A parallel workflow that runs every supported search at once and merges the results
An agent loop that calls search tools, observes each result and decides the next step
A prompt chain with a fixed search, calculate and draft sequence run on every question

explanation: Correct: C. When the number and order of steps depend on what earlier steps reveal, an agent that acts, observes tool results and re-plans is the fit; the stopping condition and tool budget become the controls to design. Why not the others: A works only when the set of paths is small and known; B wastes calls on searches most questions do not need; D cannot adapt when a search returns nothing useful.

prompt: A bank's customer-messaging assistant receives a mix of balance questions, fraud reports, mortgage enquiries and complaints. Each type needs different tools, a different tone and different escalation rules, and the team wants to tune one type without regressing the others. Which workflow pattern addresses this most directly?

options.text: Evaluator-optimizer: one model drafts the reply and another critiques it until it passes
Prompt chaining: each message runs through tone, tool and escalation steps in one order
Parallelisation: four specialist prompts answer every message and a vote picks the reply
Routing: a first call classifies each message and routes it to the prompt for that type

explanation: Correct: D. Routing separates concerns: each downstream prompt stays small and specific, and changing the complaints handler cannot affect the mortgage handler. Why not the others: A improves one reply's quality but does not separate the four cases; B forces a single sequence onto messages that need different tools and rules; C quadruples cost and lets the wrong specialist's tools run on every message.

prompt: A pharmaceutical company asks Claude to review 300-page clinical study reports against a 70-item regulatory checklist in a single call. Reviewers find that items near the end of the checklist are often skipped and that findings are inconsistent between runs. What is the most effective change?

options.text: Raise the temperature so the model explores the checklist more thoroughly on each run
Have the model restate all 70 checklist items before it begins so none are forgotten
Move the single-call design to a larger model with a longer context window
Split the review into calls per checklist section over the relevant report parts

explanation: Correct: D. Skipped late items and run-to-run variance are the classic signs of a task too large for one pass. Decomposing by checklist section gives each call a bounded job and makes output comparable between runs. Why not the others: A adds randomness, the opposite of consistency; B spends tokens restating the list without reducing the work per call; C may help at the margin but leaves the overload in place.

prompt: A travel company's booking agent must coordinate flight search, hotel search, visa checks and payment, each needing its own tools and prompt. The business wants an ordered record of every step, no payment if the visa check fails, and orchestration logic that is visible and testable in code. Which design meets this?

options.text: A single agent holding all the tools and one system prompt covering all four domains
Four independent agents that watch a shared queue and act when they see a relevant task
An orchestrator in application code that calls four specialist sub-agents in sequence
A supervisor model given the four sub-agents as tools, choosing at runtime what to call

explanation: Correct: C. When orchestration must be testable in code, put the control flow in code and keep the model inside each specialist step: the code records each outcome in order and halts when a step fails. Why not the others: A reproduces the bloated single-agent context; B makes the sequence emergent, so ordering and the halt are not guaranteed; D moves control flow into the model, which the requirement rules out.

prompt: A research-synthesis product uses an orchestrator model that breaks a question into sub-questions, spawns a worker per sub-question, and writes the final report. Reports are good but cost has tripled since launch, and traces show workers repeatedly fetching the same sources. Which change best addresses the cost without changing the pattern?

options.text: Give the orchestrator a shared results store and dedupe sub-questions before spawning
Replace the workers with a single model call that answers every sub-question in one pass
Lower each worker's maximum output tokens so the repeated fetches cost less per worker
Switch the orchestrator to the smallest model so planning costs less per report

explanation: Correct: A. The waste is duplicated work between workers, so the fix is shared state and deduplication at the orchestration layer; the orchestrator-workers shape stays intact. Why not the others: B abandons the pattern and reintroduces the overload that motivated it; C trims output, but the duplicated fetches are input and tool cost; D saves little, since the orchestrator makes few calls, and risks poorer planning.

prompt: A utility company's chief operating officer lists nine possible first AI projects, from an internal policy chatbot to automated outage-cause analysis. What should most strongly determine which project the architect recommends first?

options.text: Which project shows the largest projected cost saving on paper in the business case
Which project the executive sponsor is personally most enthusiastic about championing
Which project has a measurable outcome, available data and a tolerable cost of error
Which project can run fully automated with no human review step in the loop at all

explanation: Correct: C. A first project should be one where value can be measured, the data exists and a wrong answer is recoverable; that is what lets the organisation learn and build trust. Why not the others: A looks at value but ignores data availability and recoverability; B matters for sponsorship but is not the primary criterion; D treats removing humans as the goal, which raises risk on the first delivery.

prompt: A procurement assistant has been live for a quarter. Dashboards show cost, latency and uptime, but nobody can say whether its supplier recommendations are being accepted or overridden by buyers. Which addition completes the architecture?

options.text: A feedback loop that captures buyer accept/override decisions into the evaluation set
A second model that re-scores each recommendation and flags disagreements for review
A larger context window so the assistant sees more supplier history on every request
A weekly export of all prompts and responses to the data team for archiving and reporting

explanation: Correct: A. An end-to-end architecture runs input, processing, output and a feedback loop; without the loop the team cannot learn whether outputs are right in production. Why not the others: B adds a second opinion but still never learns what buyers actually did; C changes inputs without measuring outcomes; D stores data but creates no signal that flows back into the system.

prompt: A manufacturer wants Claude to answer engineers' questions about 40,000 maintenance manuals that are updated by suppliers every month. Which approach gives the model access to this material in a way that stays current?

options.text: Fine-tune a model on the manuals and retrain it each time a supplier sends an update
An augmented LLM that retrieves relevant manual sections from a regularly refreshed index
Summarise all the manuals into one 150,000-token document placed in every system prompt
Ask engineers to paste the relevant manual pages into the conversation with each question

explanation: Correct: B. Retrieval over a refreshed index is the standard way to give a model large, changing knowledge: the model sees only what is relevant and the index, not the model, is what gets updated. Why not the others: A bakes knowledge into weights that go stale monthly and is costly to repeat; C cannot hold 40,000 manuals and loses detail in the summary; D moves the retrieval problem onto the user.

prompt: A single internal agent handles facilities requests, expense queries and software access requests. It has 40 tools and a 7,000-token system prompt, and it has started picking the wrong tool as capabilities were added. What should the architect do?

options.text: Add a sentence to the system prompt listing which tools belong to which domain
Split the agent by domain behind a router, each specialist with its own tools and prompt
Raise the tool-use turn limit so that the agent can recover from a wrong first tool choice
Rename every tool with a domain prefix such as `hr_` or `it_` and keep the single agent

explanation: Correct: B. Tool-selection accuracy degrades as a tool set grows and overlaps; decomposing by domain shrinks each agent's choice set and prompt, which fixes the cause. Why not the others: A is a prompt-level patch that leaves 40 tools in every call; C makes wrong choices cheaper to recover from but not rarer, and adds latency and cost; D relabels the same 40 tools without reducing the choice set.

prompt: A marketing team wants an assistant that writes product descriptions meeting a strict style guide. Drafts are usually close but fail a few rules, and a human currently fixes them by hand. The team can describe the rules precisely. Which pattern automates the fix-up most directly?

options.text: Routing: send each request to a different prompt depending on its product category
Evaluator-optimizer: a checker scores each draft on the rules and the writer revises
Parallelisation: generate five drafts at once and let the reviewer choose between them
Multi-agent: one specialist agent per style rule, each rewriting the draft in turn

explanation: Correct: B. When evaluation criteria are clear and iteration demonstrably improves output, the evaluator-optimizer loop is the fit: generate, check against explicit rules, revise, with a bounded retry count. Why not the others: A changes which prompt writes but not how violations get caught; C produces more drafts for the human to fix, not fewer; D is far more machinery than a rules check needs.

prompt: A logistics provider's leadership frames an AI programme around five pillars: efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost and performance SLAs. The architect proposes an assistant that drafts customs declarations which clerks then check. Under which pillar should the business case primarily be made, and what metric supports it?

options.text: Transformation, measured by how many new customer-facing services launch in the year
Cost, measured by the number of tokens consumed per customs declaration drafted
Efficiency, measured by clerk minutes per declaration and first-pass customs acceptance
Performance SLA, measured by the model's p95 response latency on every single declaration

explanation: Correct: C. Drafting for a human to check is an efficiency play on an existing process, and the honest metrics are time saved per unit and whether quality held, here first-pass acceptance. Why not the others: A describes a different kind of initiative that creates new offerings; B measures the solution's own running cost, not business value; D is a technical constraint to meet, not the reason to build it.

prompt: An agent that reconciles invoices against purchase orders occasionally runs for 40 tool calls on a single invoice before giving up, and a few runs have issued duplicate credit notes. The business accepts some manual fallback. Which pair of architectural controls should the architect add?

options.text: A longer system prompt on when to stop, plus a note not to issue duplicate credit notes
A turn budget with a human hand-off queue, and an idempotency key on the credit-note tool
A second supervising agent that watches the first one's actions and steps in when it errs
Removing all finance-system write tools and reverting to a drafting-only assistant

explanation: Correct: B. Agents need engineered stopping conditions and safe tools: a turn budget with an explicit fallback bounds cost, and idempotent write tools make a repeated action harmless. Why not the others: A relies on instructions to enforce what code should enforce; C adds a second non-deterministic component to police the first; D over-corrects, since the business accepted automation with fallback, not its removal.

prompt: A support team wants each inbound customer email summarised into a three-line CRM note. The CRM already fetches the customer's account record and supplies it with the email, and nothing else is needed. Which pattern fits?

options.text: A prompt chain that extracts entities, classifies the email, then writes the note
An agent loop with CRM search tools, so the model can look up whatever history it needs
An orchestrator that hands the email to a sub-agent per product line and merges the notes
A single augmented call: one prompt holding the email and account record returns the note

explanation: Correct: D. One transformation whose context is already supplied is the base case of the augmented LLM: a single call with retrieval done for it, no planning and no sequencing. Why not the others: A splits a one-step task into three calls and triples cost for no gain; B gives the model autonomy to search when the only context it needs is already provided; C adds coordination overhead to a task with no sub-tasks.

prompt: A payroll provider is planning how Claude will handle the salary-adjustment forms its clients upload. Before picking a scripted pipeline or a free-running agent loop, the architect notes down properties of the job. Which TWO point toward the scripted pipeline? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The sequence of steps is identical for every form and is known before work begins
The number of tool calls varies from one to dozens depending on intermediate results
Each step must be individually logged, validated and easy to replay after the event
Requests are open-ended and the right approach is only discovered part-way through
The model is expected to recover from unexpected tool errors by trying other approaches

explanation: Correct: A and C. A workflow is the right choice when the path is known up front and when the business needs step-level predictability, validation and replay. Why not the others: B describes variable effort that only an agent loop can decide at run time; D describes exploratory work whose path emerges mid-task; E asks for autonomous recovery, the opposite of a fixed sequence.

prompt: A venture fund wants Claude to vet startups ahead of its investment committee: market sizing, a cap-table review and an audit of the product's code. The architect must pick between one augmented agent and several cooperating agents. Which TWO facts about the work argue for several agents? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The whole task must finish in under two seconds to meet the agreed response-time target
Market, cap-table and code reviews each need their own tools and instructions
The task is a single extraction with a fixed schema applied to one document at a time
The assessments can run independently and only need combining into one view at the end
The budget per run is very small and every additional model call must be justified

explanation: Correct: B and D. Multiple agents pay off when sub-tasks need separate context and tools, so one agent's prompt would be bloated and confused, and when they can proceed in parallel and be merged. Why not the others: A argues against multi-agent, which adds coordination latency; C is a job for a single call; E argues against multi-agent, which adds calls and cost.

prompt: A retailer wants to translate the problem "our returns desk is overwhelmed" into a Claude-based solution. Which TWO activities belong to translating the business problem before any architecture is chosen? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Mapping the current returns process to find where time and errors actually occur
Selecting the embedding model used to index the product catalogue for retrieval
Writing the first version of the system prompt for the returns-desk agent
Choosing between MCP and a direct API integration for connecting to the order system
Defining what a successful outcome looks like and how it will be measured

explanation: Correct: A and E. Translating a business problem means understanding the process as it is and agreeing the measurable outcome; those decide what, if anything, to automate. Why not the others: B is a retrieval design decision that should follow from that understanding; C is implementation work that presumes the solution; D is an integration choice that belongs after the problem is framed.

prompt: A telecoms retention director asks for "a Claude solution to reduce churn". The company already has a well-validated churn-propensity model, but nobody knows why customers leave: the reasons sit in 50,000 unread cancellation notes and call transcripts a month. How should the architect translate this problem into a solution?

options.text: Replace the propensity model by having Claude score churn risk from billing data
options.explanation: Discards a validated model for a tabular task that is not the actual gap.

options.text: Build an autonomous retention agent that calls at-risk customers and offers discounts
options.explanation: Jumps to a high-risk autonomous action before the knowledge gap is addressed.

options.text: Fine-tune a model on past cancellation notes to generate synthetic transcripts for study
options.explanation: Synthetic transcripts add no insight about real customers.

options.text: Use Claude to classify and summarise the notes and transcripts into churn reason codes
options.explanation: Targets Claude at the unstructured-language bottleneck and reuses the validated model.

explanation: Correct: D. Translating the problem means locating where language understanding is the real bottleneck; prediction is solved, but the reasons for churn sit in unread free text Claude can classify at scale. Why not the others: A swaps a proven tabular model for an LLM that suits the task less; B starts autonomous customer contact before the insight exists; C makes synthetic data instead of insight into real customers.

prompt: A freight forwarder sends scanned bills of lading to Claude, which extracts consignee, weight and port codes into the booking system. Error analysis shows most wrong extractions come from faded, skewed or cropped scans, where the model fills gaps with plausible values. Which change to the end-to-end architecture best addresses this?

options.text: Add an input-quality gate that scores each scan and routes unreadable ones to a person
options.explanation: Stops bad inputs at the input stage, so the model never extracts from scans it cannot read.

options.text: Add a prompt instruction to be extra careful with poor scans and double-check port codes
options.explanation: An exhortation does not make an illegible scan legible; the guessing largely continues.

options.text: Switch extraction to the most capable model and raise the output limit so it reasons more
options.explanation: A stronger model cannot recover information physically missing from the image.

options.text: Run the extraction three times per document and keep the most frequent value per field
options.explanation: Repeated guesses on an unreadable scan can agree with each other and still be wrong.

explanation: Correct: A. End-to-end design covers the input stage as well as processing: when failures originate in unusable inputs, the right control is a gate that detects them and diverts them to a human. Why not the others: B relies on wording that cannot fix missing pixels; C spends more on a model facing the same missing information; D improves consistency, not correctness, when every run is guessing.

prompt: An online retailer uses Claude to enrich product listings with attributes such as material, care instructions and size category, writing results straight into its product information system. A few malformed entries each week have broken storefront filters and shown impossible values. Which addition to the output stage is most appropriate?

options.text: Instruct the model to return only valid values and never to invent missing attributes
options.explanation: Instructions reduce errors but give no enforcement point before bad data reaches the storefront.

options.text: Validate each output against a schema and business rules before writing, queuing failures
options.explanation: Creates an enforcement point between model output and the system of record, with a path for exceptions.

options.text: Run a nightly job that scans the product system for impossible values and removes them
options.explanation: Detects defects only after they have been live on the storefront for up to a day.

options.text: Lower the sampling temperature so that the enrichment calls return more repeatable values
options.explanation: Repeatable output can still be repeatably invalid, so the downstream system is unprotected.

explanation: Correct: B. In an end-to-end architecture the output stage should check model output before it reaches a system of record: schema and rule validation catches malformed or impossible values, and a review queue handles the exceptions. Why not the others: A is useful but unenforced; C detects problems only after customers have seen them; D affects variability, not validity, so invalid values can still be written.

prompt: A video platform uses Claude to decide whether user-uploaded descriptions breach its harassment policy. A single classification call is usually right, but on borderline items its decision flips between runs, and wrongly removing content costs creator trust. The team wants a more reliable decision per item. Which pattern fits best?

options.text: Sectioning: classify each sentence in parallel and remove the item if any is flagged
options.explanation: Sentence-level splitting loses context that harassment judgements depend on.

options.text: Prompt chaining: summarise the description, classify the summary, then write a rationale
options.explanation: Still rests on one judgement per item, so borderline instability remains.

options.text: Routing: send each description to a specialised prompt depending on its language
options.explanation: Routing handles distinct input categories, not an unstable judgement on one item.

options.text: Voting: run several independent classifications and remove only above a set threshold
options.explanation: Multiple independent judgements with a threshold give a tunable decision on borderline items.

explanation: Correct: D. Voting is the parallelisation variant that runs the same task several times for diverse outputs, and a vote threshold lets the team trade false removals against missed breaches. Why not the others: A is sectioning, which splits a task into parts rather than repeating it, and here destroys context; B still ends in a single judgement; C addresses varied inputs, not the reliability of one decision.

prompt: A wealth-management assistant uses one prompt that both screens each message for requests it must refuse, such as personalised investment advice, and drafts the reply. Screening is sometimes missed on long answers, compliance wants to tune the screening rules separately, and latency must not grow noticeably. Which design fits?

options.text: Move the screening rules to the end of the combined prompt and mark them highest priority
options.explanation: Still one call doing two jobs, so screening cannot be tuned separately.

options.text: Run the screening call first and start the answer call only once screening has passed
options.explanation: Separates the concerns but adds the full screening latency in series.

options.text: Let the answering model call a screening tool whenever it judges a message might need it
options.explanation: Leaves the decision to screen with the model that is already missing cases.

options.text: Run a dedicated screening call in parallel with the answer call and gate the reply on it
options.explanation: Sectioning gives each concern focused attention and separate tuning at near single-call latency.

explanation: Correct: D. Running a guardrail check as a separate call in parallel with the main response is the sectioning form of parallelisation: each call attends to one concern, the screening prompt can be tuned independently, and wall-clock time stays near a single call. Why not the others: A keeps both jobs in one call; B achieves separation but serialises latency; C makes screening optional and model-initiated.

prompt: A pharmaceutical literature-review agent runs dozens of searches per question and reads every returned paper in its main conversation. Halfway through long reviews it forgets the inclusion criteria and repeats searches it already ran, because its context is crowded with raw abstracts and excerpts. Which change best addresses the cause?

options.text: Move to a model with a larger context window so all raw results and instructions fit
options.explanation: More room postpones the crowding but keeps the main context full of unneeded material.

options.text: Drop the oldest tool results once the context passes a fixed size, keeping recent ones
options.explanation: Blind truncation can discard the very findings and criteria the agent needs.

options.text: Copy the inclusion criteria into every tool result so the model sees them with each paper
options.explanation: Repeating instructions treats a symptom and adds tokens to a crowded context.

options.text: Delegate searching and reading to subagents with separate contexts that return summaries
options.explanation: Subagent context isolation keeps raw material out of the main context.

explanation: Correct: D. Subagents work in their own context windows, so the bulky exploration happens there and only condensed findings flow back to the lead agent, which keeps its criteria and progress in view. Why not the others: A merely raises the ceiling on an inefficient design; B loses information indiscriminately; C repeats instructions while leaving the real cause, raw results flooding the main context, untouched.

prompt: A home insurer's chat service uses a triage agent that identifies the customer and the problem, then hands over to a specialist claims agent that receives only the customer's latest message. Customers complain that after the handoff they are asked again for their policy number, incident date and what happened. What should the architect change?

options.text: Merge the triage and claims agents into one agent so that no handoff is needed
options.explanation: Removes the symptom by giving up the specialisation that motivated the split.

options.text: Pass the claims agent the triage agent's full raw transcript, including all its tool calls
options.explanation: Fixes the gap but floods the specialist with noise its narrow role does not need.

options.text: Define a structured handoff payload: identity, collected fields, summary and open request
options.explanation: Passes exactly the state the specialist needs in a predictable form.

options.text: Tell the claims agent in its prompt not to ask for information the customer already gave
options.explanation: The specialist cannot comply because it never receives that information.

explanation: Correct: C. Handoffs between agents need an explicit contract: a structured payload carrying verified identity, gathered fields, a summary and the open request gives the specialist the state it needs without the noise. Why not the others: A abandons the benefits of specialisation; B transfers the information but also all of the triage agent's clutter; D tells the specialist to use information it never receives.

prompt: A private-equity firm runs due diligence with an orchestrator and five parallel worker agents that all read and write one shared findings document. Reviewers find sections silently overwritten, contradictory statements side by side, and no way to tell which worker wrote which claim. What is the best change to how shared state is handled?

options.text: Give each worker its own attributed output store, with the orchestrator as sole merger
options.explanation: Removes concurrent writes, keeps provenance per claim and gives conflicts a single owner.

options.text: Add a lock so only one worker edits the shared document at a time, changing nothing else
options.explanation: Prevents simultaneous edits, but later workers still overwrite and provenance stays unclear.

options.text: Run the five workers one after another so each can see and build on the earlier sections
options.explanation: Serialising independent work loses parallelism and later workers can still rewrite findings.

options.text: Instruct every worker not to modify other workers' text and to note disagreements
options.explanation: Relies on model compliance for a concurrency problem the architecture should prevent.

explanation: Correct: A. Parallel workers should not share a mutable artefact; giving each its own attributed output and making the orchestrator the single writer removes overwrites, preserves provenance and gives conflicts one owner. Why not the others: B serialises edits but not ownership, so overwrites remain; C discards parallelism without fixing ownership; D asks the model to enforce what should be structural.

prompt: A university's course-design assistant launches four subagents at once to write learning outcomes, design assessments, draft the weekly schedule and compile the reading list. Results are often inconsistent: assessments test outcomes that were never written and the schedule ignores the assessments. How should the orchestration change?

options.text: Add a fifth subagent at the end that rewrites all four outputs until they are consistent
options.explanation: Patches inconsistency after the fact and may rewrite good work.

options.text: Give each subagent a longer prompt describing what the other three are likely to produce
options.explanation: Subagents still cannot see each other's actual output, so guesses keep diverging.

options.text: Produce the learning outcomes first, pass them to dependent steps, parallelise the rest
options.explanation: Respects the dependencies while keeping parallelism where it is safe.

options.text: Have all four produce a complete course design and keep the most common choices by vote
options.explanation: Voting suits repeated judgements of one task, not assembling interdependent parts.

explanation: Correct: C. Parallelisation suits independent subtasks; when later work depends on earlier outputs, those steps must run in sequence with the outputs passed forward, and only the genuinely independent pieces run concurrently. Why not the others: A adds a costly repair pass instead of fixing the ordering; B substitutes guesses for real inputs; D applies voting to a problem of dependencies, not of judgement.

prompt: A public-sector team decomposed a planning-application assessment into 28 sequential model calls, one per micro-step such as "extract site address" and "check address format". Latency is high, small errors compound along the chain, and several steps lack the context they need to judge well. How should the decomposition be revised?

options.text: Collapse all 28 steps into one large prompt so the model sees the whole application
options.explanation: Swings to the opposite extreme and reintroduces the problems decomposition solves.

options.text: Keep all 28 steps but run as many as possible in parallel to cut total latency
options.explanation: Most steps depend on earlier results, so parallelising worsens the context problem.

options.text: Keep all 28 steps and add a validation call after each one to catch errors early
options.explanation: Doubles calls and latency while leaving steps without the context they need.

options.text: Merge tightly coupled micro-steps and split only where tools or a checkpoint differ
options.explanation: Sets boundaries where they add value, cutting hops and error compounding.

explanation: Correct: D. Good decomposition places boundaries at meaningful seams, such as a change of tool or a point where an intermediate result can be checked, rather than at every micro-action; merging coupled steps restores context and shortens the chain. Why not the others: A overcorrects and loses the benefits of decomposition; B ignores the dependencies between steps; C adds calls without restoring context.

prompt: A parcel carrier wants to automate delay notifications. For each delayed shipment the process must parse structured carrier status messages, compute a revised delivery date from timetables, interpret free-text notes from depot staff, and send the customer a clear, apologetic message. How should the work be split between Claude and code?

options.text: Code parses messages and computes dates; Claude reads the notes and drafts the message
options.explanation: Deterministic logic in code, language understanding and wording in Claude.

options.text: Claude handles every step, including timetable arithmetic, in one consistent prompt
options.explanation: Asks a language model to do arithmetic and parsing that code does more reliably.

options.text: Code handles every step, with keyword rules for depot notes and fixed message templates
options.explanation: Keyword rules handle messy free text poorly, exactly where Claude adds value.

options.text: Claude computes the revised dates and reads the notes; code templates write the messages
options.explanation: Inverts the split: model arithmetic is less reliable and templates lose tailored wording.

explanation: Correct: A. Decomposition means assigning each subtask to the right mechanism: structured parsing and date arithmetic are deterministic and belong in code, while free text and customer wording are where Claude adds value. Why not the others: B wastes tokens and adds error risk on deterministic steps; C forfeits language understanding where the data is messy; D puts the model on arithmetic and code on language.

prompt: An energy supplier's business case justifies a customer-service assistant under the cost pillar, claiming it will deflect contacts from human agents. The steering group asks for one headline metric that would genuinely evidence that claim after launch. Which should the architect propose?

options.text: The number of conversations the assistant handles each month against the prior quarter
options.explanation: Volume handled says nothing about cost if many conversations still end with a human.

options.text: Fully loaded cost per resolved contact, escalations included, against the launch baseline
options.explanation: Measures the cost outcome itself, net of the costs the solution adds.

options.text: Average tokens per conversation, tracked weekly so prompt changes can be checked
options.explanation: A useful engineering signal, but not whether the business spends less per contact.

options.text: The average customer satisfaction rating given to assistant chats in the post-chat survey
options.explanation: Satisfaction evidences experience quality, not the cost reduction claimed.

explanation: Correct: B. A value pillar is evidenced by a metric of the outcome it promises; for cost that is the fully loaded cost per resolved contact against the baseline, which counts the solution's own running costs and the escalations it fails to deflect. Why not the others: A measures activity, not savings; C is an internal efficiency indicator; D tracks a different dimension, customer experience, rather than cost.

prompt: A health insurer commits to a performance SLA: 99% of prior-authorisation requests must have a draft decision in front of a clinician within two hours of receipt. The proposed agent usually finishes in minutes, but a few cases loop through many record lookups and take far longer. How should the architecture be aligned with the SLA?

options.text: Measure p99 end to end, cap the agent's time and steps, and route overruns to clinicians
options.explanation: Measures the committed percentile and bounds the tail with a fallback.

options.text: Report the average processing time weekly, since most cases finish well inside two hours
options.explanation: An average hides the long tail that the 99% commitment is about.

options.text: Move every case to an overnight batch run, with clinicians picking up drafts next morning
options.explanation: Cheaper, but overnight turnaround breaks a two-hour commitment for most requests.

options.text: Switch all cases to the fastest model, accepting lower draft quality to finish in time
options.explanation: Speeds up calls but does not bound looping cases, and sacrifices quality.

explanation: Correct: A. An SLA stated as a percentile must be measured as that percentile across the whole journey, and long-tail agent runs need a hard budget with a defined fallback so the commitment holds even when the agent struggles. Why not the others: B reports a metric that conceals the tail; C optimises cost at the expense of the time commitment; D trades away quality and still leaves runaway loops unbounded.

prompt: A bank's operations team is agreeing a service-level agreement for a Claude-based service that triages incoming trade-finance documents for downstream teams. Which TWO items belong in the performance SLA? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A per-document latency target at a stated percentile, measured at the service boundary
options.explanation: A percentile target at the boundary reflects what downstream teams actually experience.

options.text: A minimum triage accuracy measured on a refreshed, labelled sample of production documents
options.explanation: Quality is part of performance and needs a measurable threshold on real traffic.

options.text: The exact prompt wording and number of examples the triage prompt must always contain
options.explanation: Implementation details belong in design documents, not in an outcome-based SLA.

options.text: The provider's published benchmark scores for the model version the service currently uses
options.explanation: Generic benchmarks do not measure this service's performance on its own documents.

options.text: A cap on the number of agents and tools in the architecture so the design cannot grow
options.explanation: Architecture size is an internal design choice, not a service outcome.

explanation: Correct: A and B. A performance SLA should state measurable outcomes that consumers of the service experience: latency at a percentile measured end to end, and a quality threshold measured on labelled samples of real traffic. Why not the others: C fixes implementation details the team must stay free to change; D cites benchmarks that ignore these documents; E caps design choices rather than service outcomes.

prompt: A claims-handling assistant drafts settlement letters that adjusters review and edit before sending. The architect is designing the feedback loop so that the solution improves over time in a controlled way. Which TWO elements best close that loop? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Retain every raw prompt and response in cold storage, unlinked to the adjuster's actions
options.explanation: Storage alone, without outcome data, gives nothing to learn from.

options.text: Let the assistant rewrite its own system prompt nightly from adjusters' thumbs-up ratings
options.explanation: Uncontrolled self-modification bypasses evaluation and can silently regress behaviour.

options.text: Capture every adjuster's edits and override reasons, linked to the traces of those drafts
options.explanation: Links real outcomes to specific outputs, giving actionable signal.

options.text: Add representative failures from reviewed cases to the regression set run before changes
options.explanation: Turns production lessons into tests that gate future changes.

options.text: Build a dashboard of uptime, volume and token spend, reviewed weekly by the platform team
options.explanation: Operational health metrics say nothing about whether the drafts are good.

explanation: Correct: C and D. A controlled feedback loop captures outcome signal tied to specific outputs and feeds it back into the evaluation set that gates future changes, so the system improves without regressing. Why not the others: A stores data without outcomes; B closes the loop without any evaluation gate, risking silent regressions; E monitors operations rather than output quality.

prompt: A mortgage lender's agent prepares decisions on loan-modification requests. Approvals below a set amount are low-risk and reversible; anything above it, and every denial, has legal consequences for the customer. The team wants real automation without exposing the lender to unreviewed harm. Where should human review sit?

options.text: Review every output before release, so that no decision reaches a customer unreviewed
Review a random 5% sample of all decisions each week to estimate the agent's error rate
Let the agent decide for itself when a case is unusual enough to escalate to a human
Gate denials and above-threshold approvals on human sign-off, auto-releasing the rest

explanation: Correct: D. Human review belongs where an error is costly or irreversible; gating consequential decisions while auto-releasing low-risk, reversible ones keeps the benefit of automation without unreviewed harm. Why not the others: A reviews everything and removes most of the value of automating; B measures quality after the fact but lets harm reach customers; C leaves escalation to the component being checked.

prompt: A legal publisher builds retrieval over 200,000 contracts. Answers are often wrong when a clause's meaning depends on a term defined elsewhere in the same contract, and retrieved chunks frequently begin or end mid-sentence. Which TWO changes to the retrieval design most directly address these failures? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Chunk on clause and section boundaries rather than on a fixed number of characters
Reduce the number of retrieved chunks to one so the model is not distracted by extras
Fine-tune the model on the contract corpus so that retrieval is no longer needed
Prefix each chunk with document context such as the contract title and defined terms
Increase the embedding dimensions so that semantically similar clauses score higher

explanation: Correct: A and D. Fixed-size chunks split sentences and clauses, so aligning boundaries to the document's structure keeps each unit whole, and prefixing each chunk with context from its parent document lets the model resolve terms defined elsewhere. Why not the others: B starves the model of supporting clauses; C replaces retrieval with weights that go stale; E changes scoring, not chunk content.

prompt: A marketplace screens 1.5 million new listings a day for policy violations. On the team's labelled set the three Claude model tiers score within half a point of one another, and the pipeline must finish each night on a fixed budget. Which model choice is best?

options.text: The largest tier, since a few listings each night will be harder than the test set
A random mix of tiers per listing, so that the night's cost and latency average out
The middle tier, as a safe default between capability and cost for a production system
The smallest tier, since measured accuracy is equal and it is the cheapest and fastest

explanation: Correct: D. Model selection follows measured task performance: when the labelled set shows no meaningful accuracy gap, the smallest tier delivers the same quality at the lowest cost and latency, as a fixed-budget nightly batch requires. Why not the others: A pays for capability the evaluation says is unused; B adds unpredictable behaviour and cost for no gain; C hedges a choice the data has already settled.

prompt: A legal-drafting feature needs to follow a 30-page playbook, reason about exceptions, and produce long documents, and it runs a few hundred times a day. The team is comparing the most capable Claude model with a mid-tier one. What should drive the decision?

options.text: Default to the mid-tier model, as capability differences rarely matter in drafting work
Pick whichever model has the larger context window, since the playbook runs to 30 pages
Run both on representative cases and weigh the quality gap against cost at this volume
Pick the most capable model outright, because errors in legal drafting are costly

explanation: Correct: C. The choice is an evidence-based trade-off: measure the quality gap on real drafting cases, then judge whether it justifies the extra cost and latency, which at a few hundred runs a day is small in absolute terms. Why not the others: A and D decide by rule of thumb rather than data; B selects on a dimension that may not differ between the candidates and says nothing about drafting quality.

prompt: A retailer's shopping assistant opens its system prompt with a personalised line naming the customer and their loyalty tier, followed by 8,000 tokens of fixed catalogue rules with a cache breakpoint after them. Cache reads are almost zero. Why?

options.text: Catalogue rules of that size exceed what one breakpoint can cache and need splitting up
The cache matches an exact prefix, and the personalised opening differs per customer
Cache reads require the user message to be identical to that of the previous request
The breakpoint belongs at the start of the system prompt rather than after the rules

explanation: Correct: B. A cache read needs the prompt to match a stored prefix exactly up to the breakpoint. A customer-specific opening makes each prefix unique, so nothing is reused; moving it after the rules restores hits. Why not the others: A is backwards, as large static blocks are what caching is for; C is wrong because content after the breakpoint does not affect the match; D would cache nothing useful.

prompt: A bank's platform team switched on step-by-step reasoning for every prompt. A loan-eligibility explainer that weighs several rules got clearly better; a lookup that pulls an IBAN out of an email is now slower and dearer at unchanged accuracy. What should the architect do?

options.text: Keep step-by-step reasoning everywhere so that all prompts follow one house pattern
Remove it from the eligibility explainer as well, since it adds cost and latency there
Keep reasoning for the rule-weighing task and use a direct prompt for the IBAN lookup
Swap reasoning for few-shot examples on every prompt, as examples are cheaper per call

explanation: Correct: C. Prompting techniques are matched to the task: step-by-step reasoning pays off where there are rules to weigh and is pure overhead on a single-field lookup, so the two endpoints should use different prompts. Why not the others: A buys reasoning the lookup never uses; B discards a measured quality gain; D applies another technique uniformly instead of fitting technique to task.

prompt: An airline's booking assistant has a hard rule (never confirm a refund amount) midway through 15,000 tokens of fare-rule reference in its system prompt. The rule is skipped on roughly one call in ten, and rephrasing it made no difference. What change is most likely to fix this?

options.text: Repeat the rule verbatim at several points inside the fare-rule reference material
Put the rule in a delimited instructions block up top and restate it after the data
Raise the temperature so that the model weighs every part of the prompt more evenly
Have each caller include the rule in their message so it is the most recent instruction

explanation: Correct: B. Instructions buried inside long reference content lose salience. Separating rules from data with delimiters, placing them first and restating critical ones at the end is the standard fix. Why not the others: A adds repetition without structure and dilutes the reference further; C increases sampling randomness, not adherence; D leaves a system guardrail to each caller and exposes it to tampering.

prompt: A pharmaceutical company generates batch-release certificates in a fixed layout: section order, exact heading names and a results table in a set column order. A prose description of the layout gets it nearly right but not every time. Which technique most directly fixes this?

options.text: Include two or three complete certificates in the exact layout as few-shot examples
Ask the model to reason step by step about the required layout before it starts writing
Move to a larger model and keep the prose description of the layout as it stands
Lower the output token limit so that the model has less room to stray from the layout

explanation: Correct: A. Showing the format beats describing it: complete few-shot examples pin down section order, heading names and table layout in a way prose cannot. Why not the others: B helps on reasoning tasks, not on reproducing a layout; C may improve adherence a little but leaves the ambiguity of a prose spec in place; D truncates output instead of shaping it.

prompt: A law firm's assistant answers questions about 200,000 tokens of lease agreements by loading the whole set into context on every request. Answers drawn from leases in the middle of the set are noticeably less accurate, and each request is slow and costly. What is the best remedy?

options.text: Retrieve only the leases relevant to each question and place them, labelled, in context
Keep the full set in context and instruct the model to attend closely to the middle leases
Split each request into two calls carrying half the leases each and merge the two answers
Compress the leases by stripping headings, clause numbers and whitespace to save tokens

explanation: Correct: A. Supply the right tokens, not all of them: retrieving the relevant leases cuts cost and latency and removes the mid-context quality dip by giving the model a focused, labelled set. Why not the others: B tries to instruct around a structural problem; C doubles the calls and still cannot tell which half holds the answer; D saves few tokens while destroying the structure used to locate clauses.

prompt: An agent must apply a 9,000-token procedure for reconciling bank statements, but only about one request in twenty is a reconciliation. The team currently loads the procedure into every system prompt. Which approach keeps the capability while reducing per-request tokens?

options.text: Package the procedure as a Skill whose description triggers loading it only when needed
Keep the procedure in every prompt and enable caching so the repeated tokens cost less
Summarise the procedure to about 500 tokens and accept less detail on reconciliations
Ask users to say up front whether a request is a reconciliation so a prompt can be picked

explanation: Correct: A. Skills use progressive disclosure: the model sees only each Skill's name and description and loads the full instructions when a request matches, so the 9,000 tokens are paid only on the one request in twenty that needs them. Why not the others: B lowers the price of the waste but still sends the tokens every time; C discards the detail a procedure exists to supply; D pushes a routing decision onto users.

prompt: A payments company's support assistant must answer only questions about its own product and decline anything else. The team is designing a system prompt to act as that guardrail. Which design is most robust?

options.text: A single sentence asking the model to be helpful and to stay on topic with the customer
Role and scope with examples and a set refusal behaviour, plus a check on output in code
A list of forbidden keywords in the system prompt that the model must never respond to
A firm warning that off-topic replies are unacceptable, repeated at the end of the prompt

explanation: Correct: B. A guardrail prompt is specific: a role, an explicit scope with examples on both sides of the line, a defined refusal behaviour, and a check outside the model because a prompt alone can be talked around. Why not the others: A is too vague to be applied consistently; C is brittle and both over- and under-blocks; D states the goal without defining the scope or what a refusal looks like.

prompt: A ticketing marketplace's assistant sends a 7,000-token system prompt on each of 2 million calls a day, most of them simple order-status checks. Input tokens dominate the bill. Which TWO changes most directly cut cost per request without reducing capability? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Drop the examples section and rely on the model to infer the required output format alone
Raise max output tokens on every request so that no response is ever cut short
Order the prompt so static content comes first and enable caching on that prefix
Send each request to two models in parallel and keep whichever response was cheaper
Route order-status checks to a smaller model that evaluation shows handles them as well

explanation: Correct: C and E. Caching a stable prefix means the 7,000 repeated tokens are read at a fraction of the price, and routing the simple majority to the smallest model that measurably does the job removes capability spend where it is not needed. Why not the others: A cuts tokens by removing something that was there for quality; B does nothing for input cost and may raise output cost; D doubles the spend.

prompt: A procurement assistant's system prompt grew for a year and now mixes rules, supplier data and sample outputs in one block. Behaviour varies between calls on the same kind of request. Which TWO changes would most improve how consistently it follows instructions? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Cut the instructions to the fewest possible words, even where that leaves cases implicit
Separate instructions, supplier data and examples with clear delimiters or XML tags
Put the most important rule mid-prompt where it is surrounded by supporting context
Raise the temperature so the model handles varied inputs more flexibly and naturally
Replace vague directives with explicit statements of desired behaviour and edge cases

explanation: Correct: B and E. Clear structure lets the model tell instructions from data and examples, and explicit, specific instructions that cover the edge cases remove the ambiguity that produces call-to-call variation. Why not the others: A leaves cases implicit, which is where inconsistency comes from; C buries the rule at the position of weakest attention; D increases output variability rather than reducing it.

prompt: A team wants a model to extract three fields from a short delivery note. The task is simple, the fields are unambiguous and the team has no labelled examples yet. Which prompting approach should they try first?

options.text: Zero-shot: a clear instruction naming the three fields and the required output format
Chain-of-thought: have the model reason at length about the note before extracting
Few-shot: a twenty-example prompt built from synthetic notes the team writes itself
Free text: ask for a prose summary of the note and parse the fields out of it in code

explanation: Correct: A. Start simple: a precise zero-shot instruction usually suffices for an unambiguous extraction and is the cheapest to run and iterate on; add examples or reasoning only when evaluation shows a gap. Why not the others: B adds tokens and latency to a task with nothing to reason through; C front-loads effort on synthetic data before knowing it is needed; D discards direct field output and adds fragile parsing.

prompt: An insurer runs multi-step reinsurance scenarios through Claude. The prompt says "think step by step" and dictates a rigid 20-step script, yet answers on the hardest cases stay shallow. The team wants deeper reasoning at controllable cost. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Extend the script to 40 numbered steps so every sub-calculation is covered in fixed order
options.explanation: A longer prescriptive script adds rigidity, not depth, and gives no control over reasoning cost.

options.text: Enable extended thinking with a tuned budget and swap the script for high-level guidance
options.explanation: Extended thinking gives a tunable reasoning phase; high-level guidance usually beats a step script.

options.text: Raise the temperature on hard scenarios so the model explores more reasoning paths
options.explanation: Temperature adds sampling randomness; it does not make the model reason more thoroughly.

options.text: Move all reasoning into the final answer and drop the separate thinking section entirely
options.explanation: This changes where reasoning appears, not how deep it goes, and clutters the deliverable.

explanation: Correct: B. Extended thinking gives Claude a dedicated reasoning phase whose depth is tunable via a token budget or effort setting, so quality can be traded against cost on an eval set, and broad guidance tends to beat a rigid step script. Why not the others: A makes the script more rigid without adding depth control; C only adds sampling randomness; D relocates the reasoning rather than deepening it.

prompt: A consultancy queries Claude about 60,000-token tender packs. The prompt opens with the question, then pastes all the documents as one undifferentiated block. Answers are often vague and attribute requirements to the wrong document. Which restructuring is most likely to help?

options.text: Place tagged documents with sources first, the question last, and ask for quotes first
options.explanation: Long material above the query, per-document tags with sources and quote-first grounding are best practice.

options.text: Keep the question at the top and restate it in capitals so it gets top priority
options.explanation: Emphasis does not fix the ordering or the missing document boundaries that cause the mix-ups.

options.text: Strip the document headers and merge the files so the pack reads as a single specification
options.explanation: Removing boundaries and sources makes attribution errors more likely, not less.

options.text: Ask one question per document in separate calls and stitch the answers together in code
options.explanation: Per-document calls lose the cross-document view a tender question usually needs and multiply cost.

explanation: Correct: A. Anthropic's long-context guidance is to place long documents near the top with the query at the end, to wrap each document in its own tags with source metadata, and to have the model extract relevant quotes before answering. Why not the others: B adds emphasis without fixing structure; C removes the boundaries needed to attribute requirements; D fragments the pack and multiplies calls.

prompt: An HR policy assistant sends a 9,000-token stable prefix with a cache breakpoint after it. Requests arrive only every 10 to 20 minutes. Nearly every request pays a cache write and very few get reads, so caching costs more than it saves. What is the most appropriate change?

options.text: Add three more breakpoints inside the prefix so it is cached as smaller reusable segments
options.explanation: More breakpoints do not help when every entry has expired before the next request arrives.

options.text: Use the one-hour cache lifetime, as the request gaps exceed the default five-minute one
options.explanation: The default entry expires between requests; a one-hour lifetime keeps the prefix warm across the gaps.

options.text: Move the breakpoint to the end of the user message so whole requests are stored for reuse
options.explanation: The user message differs every time, so caching it adds writes that are never read.

options.text: Turn caching off, since it only pays off for apps handling many requests every second
options.explanation: Caching pays off whenever reuse falls within the lifetime; a longer lifetime fits this traffic.

explanation: Correct: B. The default cache lifetime is five minutes, refreshed on each read; with 10 to 20 minute gaps the entry expires and every request pays a write premium. The one-hour lifetime costs more per write but turns most requests into reads. Why not the others: A adds segments that expire just the same; C caches content that never repeats; D abandons a saving available once the lifetime matches the cadence.

prompt: A multi-tenant agent sends one 6,000-token system prompt on every request, with a breakpoint after it. To enforce entitlements, the app builds the `tools` array per tenant and names the tenant in each description. System-prompt cache reads are near zero. What is the cause and fix?

options.text: The system prompt is too large to cache in one piece; split it across several breakpoints
options.explanation: There is no size problem here; the prefix already differs before the system prompt is reached.

options.text: Cache entries are per tenant; switch to the one-hour lifetime so they last between visits
options.explanation: Tenancy is not the cause; the per-tenant tools array changes the prefix, so a longer lifetime still misses.

options.text: Tools lead the cached prefix; send one stable tool set and enforce entitlements in code
options.explanation: Changing tool definitions invalidates everything after them; entitlements belong in code anyway.

options.text: Caching ignores tools; add a breakpoint on the last user message so history is cached
options.explanation: Tools are part of the cached prefix, and a later breakpoint cannot hit when the earlier prefix differs.

explanation: Correct: C. The cached prefix is built in the order tools, system, messages, and a change at one level invalidates it and everything after it, so per-tenant tool arrays defeat the system-prompt cache. One stable tool set with authorisation in the handlers restores hits. Why not the others: A misdiagnoses a size issue; B blames tenancy when the prefix itself differs; D is wrong because tools are part of the prefix.

prompt: A university team wrote a lab-report grading Skill. Its description reads "Lab report helper"; guidance on when to use it sits in the SKILL.md body and the rubric in a bundled file. In testing Claude rarely uses it, even when asked to grade a report. What should the team change?

options.text: Move the rubric and bundled files into the SKILL.md body so everything is visible up front
options.explanation: The SKILL.md body is only read after the Skill triggers, so this does not help it trigger and bloats it.

options.text: Make the description say what the Skill does and when to use it; only that is seen first
options.explanation: Before triggering, only the metadata is in context, and the description is what requests are matched against.

options.text: Paste the SKILL.md and rubric into every system prompt so the guidance is always present
options.explanation: This abandons progressive disclosure and pays the token cost on every request.

options.text: Turn the rubric into an executable script, since Skills only trigger when they bundle code
options.explanation: Scripts are optional resources; triggering depends on the description, not on bundled code.

explanation: Correct: B. Skills use progressive disclosure: only name and description load at startup, the SKILL.md body enters context when the Skill triggers, and bundled files are read only as needed. A vague description gives nothing to match requests against. Why not the others: A edits content that is invisible until after triggering; C defeats the token savings Skills exist for; D rests on a false premise about scripts.

prompt: A route-planning agent makes hundreds of tool calls per session over large schedule files. Late in long runs it slows, costs climb and it hits the context limit, though most old tool results are stale; a few early findings are needed later. Which approach best sustains long runs?

options.text: Move to a model with a larger context window and keep every tool result in the history
options.explanation: This postpones the limit while cost and latency keep growing with every stale result carried forward.

options.text: Truncate every tool result to its first 200 characters the moment it returns, before use
options.explanation: The agent loses data it has not yet processed, which harms planning quality.

options.text: Clear old tool results past a threshold; the agent keeps key findings in a memory file
options.explanation: Clearing stale results bounds context, and the memory file preserves the few facts needed later.

options.text: Restart the agent with an empty context whenever it nears the limit and redo earlier work
options.explanation: Restarting discards progress and repeats tool calls, raising cost instead of cutting it.

explanation: Correct: C. Context editing that clears the oldest tool results past a threshold removes material the agent has already processed, and pairing it with a memory file (or compaction) keeps the few findings that matter later, so long runs stay within budget. Why not the others: A treats capacity as the fix while cost keeps climbing; B discards data before it has been used; D throws away progress and repeats work.

prompt: A travel platform handles booking changes with Claude. About 85% are simple date changes; the rest involve multi-leg itineraries and partner fare rules. The top model meets quality targets but is too slow and costly at peak. Which design best balances cost, latency and quality?

options.text: Run every request on the smallest model and retry each failed request up to five times
options.explanation: Blind retries do not supply missing capability for complex cases and add latency to them.

options.text: Route date changes to a smaller model; escalate complex or failed cases to the larger one
options.explanation: Tiering by difficulty spends capability only where needed, with evaluation confirming each tier.

options.text: Let customers pick a fast or a thorough model in the interface and own the trade-off
options.explanation: Customers cannot judge which model their request needs; this pushes an architectural decision onto users.

options.text: Keep the largest model for every request but halve the maximum output length to save cost
options.explanation: Capping output risks truncated answers and leaves input cost and model latency largely unchanged.

explanation: Correct: B. Model tiering sends the routine majority to a smaller model and escalates complex or check-failing requests to the larger one, with evaluation confirming each tier meets the quality bar. Why not the others: A relies on retries that cannot add capability; C hands an engineering trade-off to customers who cannot judge it; D trims output, risking truncation without touching the main cost driver.

prompt: A media company summarises podcast transcripts that range from a few thousand to several hundred thousand tokens. The pipeline estimates size as characters divided by four; some requests overflow the context window while others are chunked needlessly. What should the team do?

options.text: Lower the assumed characters-per-token ratio to two so the estimate is more conservative
options.explanation: A cruder heuristic still mis-estimates and would chunk far more transcripts than necessary.

options.text: Send each transcript as is, catch the error, and chunk and resend only the rejected ones
options.explanation: Using failures as the size check wastes calls and latency when size can be measured beforehand.

options.text: Split each transcript into fixed 10,000-token chunks regardless of its length, to be safe
options.explanation: Chunking short transcripts needlessly fragments them and adds extra merge steps.

options.text: Count tokens with the API first and chunk only when input plus output exceeds the window
options.explanation: Measuring tokens directly avoids both overflows and needless chunking.

explanation: Correct: D. The token-counting endpoint returns the input token count for a prospective request, including system prompt and tools, so the pipeline can decide accurately whether a transcript plus room for output fits before sending it. Why not the others: A swaps one heuristic for another and over-chunks; B uses errors as a measurement tool and wastes calls; C chunks every transcript regardless of need.

prompt: A bank runs twelve customer-letter prompts that differ only in product, rules and customer details; each was hand-edited and they have drifted apart. The architect wants one maintainable, testable design that keeps customer data apart from instructions. Which fits best?

options.text: Merge the twelve into one prompt covering every product and let the model pick what fits
options.explanation: One sprawling prompt dilutes relevant instructions and makes changes for one product risky for all.

options.text: Keep each team's own prompt but circulate edits weekly so changes spread across variants
options.explanation: Manual propagation is what caused the drift; it does not create a single source of truth.

options.text: Splice customer details directly into the instruction sentences so the prompt reads well
options.explanation: Mixing data into instructions blurs the boundary the architect wants and invites confusion.

options.text: One versioned template: fixed instructions first, then XML-tagged variables for the data
options.explanation: A template gives one source of truth, tagged variables separate data, and a static prefix suits caching.

explanation: Correct: D. A single versioned template keeps the fixed instructions in one place and fills product and customer variables at run time; XML tags around the variables separate data from instructions, and static content first makes the prefix cacheable. Why not the others: A creates a bloated catch-all prompt; B is the manual process that caused the drift; C merges data into instructions, the opposite of the goal.

prompt: A hospital is building a discharge-summary assistant. The architect must decide where to put the assistant's role as a documentation aide and its standing rules, and where to put each patient's notes and the summary request. Which placement follows recommended practice?

options.text: Role, rules, patient notes and the request in the system prompt, with an empty user turn
options.explanation: Per-request data belongs in the user turn; stuffing it into the system prompt defeats reuse and caching.

options.text: Role and rules in the system prompt, the patient's notes and the request in the user turn
options.explanation: The system prompt carries the stable role and rules; task-specific content goes in the user turn.

options.text: Omit the role, since a role only changes tone and not accuracy in specialist domains
options.explanation: Role prompting can improve focus and domain performance, not just tone.

options.text: Role and rules in each user turn and an empty system prompt, so the model has less to read
options.explanation: Repeating stable rules per turn gains nothing and loses the system prompt's role-setting purpose.

explanation: Correct: B. Anthropic recommends the system prompt to set Claude's role and the stable rules that apply to every request, and putting task-specific instructions and data, here the notes and the request, in the user turn. Why not the others: A puts changing data into the system prompt and defeats reuse; C underrates role prompting, which can improve accuracy; D moves stable rules out of their intended place.

prompt: A retailer extracts product attributes from supplier text into JSON. The old design prefilled the assistant turn with an opening brace, but the new model version rejects prefill, and responses now sometimes carry a preamble or invalid JSON. Which approach is most reliable?

options.text: Constrain output with structured outputs or a tool whose schema defines the attributes
options.explanation: Schema-constrained output removes preambles and malformed JSON at the source.

options.text: Stay on the older model version so the prefill keeps working, and postpone the migration
options.explanation: This defers the problem and forgoes the newer model's improvements without fixing the format.

options.text: Add a capitalised sentence demanding JSON only, and log failures for manual repair
options.explanation: Stronger wording reduces but does not eliminate format errors, and manual repair does not scale.

options.text: Strip text before the first brace with a regex and accept that malformed objects are lost
options.explanation: Post-processing hides preambles but silently loses records when the JSON itself is invalid.

explanation: Correct: A. When output must parse, constrain it: structured outputs with a JSON schema, or a tool whose input schema defines the attributes, make valid schema-shaped JSON the response format instead of hoping the model complies. Why not the others: B blocks the migration without solving the problem; C relies on emphasis and manual clean-up; D treats the symptom and silently drops data whenever the JSON is invalid.

prompt: An energy retailer's support agent sends tool definitions, a long instruction block, a knowledge-base section refreshed hourly, and a growing conversation history on each turn. Cache hit rates are disappointing. Which TWO design choices most improve cache reuse? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Order segments by stability with a breakpoint each, so a refresh only affects later ones
options.explanation: A change invalidates only its own segment and those after it, so stable segments placed first stay cached.

options.text: Put a timestamp at the top of the instructions so the model knows the data is fresh
options.explanation: A changing value early in the prefix invalidates everything after it on every request.

options.text: Use a single breakpoint at the start of the prompt so the cache covers the whole request
options.explanation: A breakpoint caches the prefix up to that point; placing it at the start caches almost nothing.

options.text: Send only the tools relevant to each turn, adding and removing them as topics change
options.explanation: Tool definitions head the prefix, so changing them each turn invalidates the entire cache.

options.text: Keep tool choice and thinking settings fixed across turns; changes invalidate messages
options.explanation: These settings are part of the cache key for message blocks, so varying them forces fresh writes.

explanation: Correct: A and E. The prefix is ordered tools, system, messages, and a change invalidates its level and all after it, so stability-ordered segments with a breakpoint each let an hourly refresh leave earlier segments cached; tool choice or thinking changes invalidate cached messages. Why not the others: B puts a changing value early in the prefix; C caches almost nothing; D changes the first prefix level every turn.

prompt: A government benefits agency classifies incoming letters into 15 case types. Zero-shot results confuse several similar types, so the team is adding few-shot examples to the prompt. Which TWO practices should guide how they write the examples? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Choose examples that vary in wording, length and case type, including the confusable pairs
options.explanation: Diverse, relevant examples covering the hard distinctions teach the boundary rather than a surface pattern.

options.text: Repeat one example with small wording changes so the model sees one consistent pattern
options.explanation: Near-identical examples encourage overfitting to one pattern and teach nothing about the confused types.

options.text: Wrap each example in <example> tags to keep it apart from instructions and the live letter
options.explanation: Tagging examples keeps them distinct from instructions and live input, reducing confusion.

options.text: Pick examples only from the most common case type, since those dominate production traffic
options.explanation: Examples from one type do nothing to resolve confusion between the similar, less common types.

options.text: Give only the output label in each example, since the letter text just adds tokens
options.explanation: Examples teach by pairing input with output; labels alone show nothing about the boundary.

explanation: Correct: A and C. Few-shot examples should be relevant and diverse, covering the distinctions the model gets wrong so it does not latch onto one pattern, and wrapped in <example> tags so they stay apart from instructions and input. Why not the others: B and D make the example set narrow, teaching nothing about the confusable types; E strips the input half of each example, leaving nothing to learn the boundary from.

prompt: A publisher must tag 3 million archive articles with a controlled vocabulary once, then 20,000 new articles a day. The largest Claude model tags accurately but is too costly for the backfill; the smallest is cheap but misses subtle categories. Which approach is most defensible?

options.text: Run the largest model on everything and stretch the backfill over as many months as needed
Use the largest model to build few-shot examples, then run the smallest that passes eval
Run the smallest model on everything with today's prompt and accept the subtle misses
Run the smallest model on the backfill and the largest on new articles, which matter more

explanation: Correct: B. The capable model is used where it adds most value, producing examples and a reference set, and the cheaper model carries the volume once evaluation shows the gap is closed. Why not the others: A spends the premium model's cost on every article when only the examples need it; C locks in a known quality shortfall; D applies two quality bars to one vocabulary and still pays the premium daily.

prompt: A retailer wants Claude applications from four product teams to share integrations with twenty internal systems, each owned by a different team. Systems are added and retired every quarter. Which integration approach fits best?

options.text: Each application embeds its own API client for every system it uses
Applications call each other's agents to borrow missing integrations
One central team ships a single library that wraps all twenty systems
Each system team publishes an MCP server that applications connect to
