explanation: Correct: D. MCP fits many systems, many consumers and frequent churn: each owning team exposes its system once and every application discovers and reuses it. Why not the others: A repeats the integration work per application; B couples applications to one another for no architectural reason; C moves ownership away from the teams that know the systems and creates a release bottleneck.

prompt: A field-operations agent has accumulated 60 tools across eight departments. Selection accuracy has dropped, each call is slower, and logs show a third of the tools have never been invoked in production. What should the architect do first?

options.text: Prune the unused tools and scope the rest so each request sees its own area
Expand every tool description so the model can distinguish all 60 tools
Raise the output token limit so the model can reason longer about selection
Move to the largest available model, which copes better with big tool sets

explanation: Correct: A. This is capability bloat: every registered tool costs tokens and dilutes selection on every call, so remove what is unused and present only the relevant subset per request. Why not the others: B invests in descriptions for tools that should not be there; C adds latency without reducing the confusion; D pays more to tolerate a catalogue that keeps growing.

prompt: A benefits assistant answers staff questions about their own pension records. It uses one service account that can read everyone's data, and the system prompt tells the model to return only the asker's records. A security review flags this. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Add a second system-prompt rule that forbids access to any other employee's data
Log every query with the asking employee's ID so misuse can be investigated afterwards
Pass the caller's identity to the tool layer and let the pensions API enforce the scope
Switch to a model that follows system-prompt rules more reliably under adversarial input

explanation: Correct: C. Authorisation must be enforced below the model, in the tool or API layer, using the caller's real identity; a prompt is not an access-control mechanism and can be manipulated. Why not the others: A and D keep the control in the prompt, which is the gap the review found; B is a detective control that notices disclosure only after it has happened.

prompt: A RAG assistant over reinsurance treaties uses fixed 250-token chunks. Retrieved chunks are often clause fragments whose meaning depends on definitions elsewhere in the treaty, and answers suffer. Which chunking change addresses this?

options.text: Shrink chunks to 100 tokens so retrieval matches the relevant clause more precisely
Chunk by clause and section, with overlap and a document and section header on each
Index each whole treaty as one chunk so clauses are never separated from definitions
Keep 250-token chunks but retrieve the top 50 instead of the top 5 for fuller context

explanation: Correct: B. Chunking should follow the shape of the data: clause-aligned chunks with overlap and a contextual header keep each clause intact and tell the model which treaty and section it came from. Why not the others: A makes the fragments smaller and worse; C produces chunks too large to retrieve precisely or to fit several of in context; D floods the context with fragments instead of fixing them.

prompt: A laboratory-supplies assistant uses purely semantic vector retrieval. Free-text questions work well, but searches for exact catalogue codes such as "LB-4420-K" often return similar-looking but wrong items. Which retrieval strategy fixes this?

options.text: Replace vector retrieval with keyword search only, since codes are the harder case
Increase the embedding dimension so codes are represented more precisely
Ask users to describe items in words instead of entering catalogue codes
Hybrid retrieval that combines the semantic index with a lexical index for codes

explanation: Correct: D. Retrieval should match the query pattern: embeddings capture meaning but not exact strings, while lexical search matches identifiers precisely, so combining both serves both query types. Why not the others: A fixes codes but breaks the free-text queries that already work; B does not turn embeddings into exact matching; C pushes the system's failure onto users.

prompt: Adding a re-ranking step to an internal IT-helpdesk assistant raises answer accuracy from 84% to 91% and adds 400 ms. The agreed response-time SLA is 2.5 seconds and current p95 latency is 1.4 seconds. What should the architect decide?

options.text: Reject it, because any added latency erodes the margin against the SLA
Adopt it: the gain is material, p95 stays inside the SLA, and record the decision
Adopt it only for requests that arrive outside business hours when traffic is lower
Run it asynchronously and replace the answer on screen once re-ranking completes

explanation: Correct: B. An accuracy-latency trade-off is settled with numbers: a 7-point gain for 400 ms leaves p95 near 1.8 seconds against a 2.5-second SLA, a clear win worth documenting. Why not the others: A treats latency as the only metric; C makes answer quality depend on the clock; D shows users a worse answer first and complicates the experience for no latency reason.

prompt: An insurer's claims agents handle 80,000 conversations a day. Each one is dumped verbatim, with every tool input and output, into a storage bucket; the bill keeps growing, and when a claim goes wrong it still takes hours to find the conversation. How should tracing be set up at this volume?

options.text: Stop logging prompts and responses and keep only daily aggregate error counts
Keep full payload logging but shorten retention to a single day to reduce the storage bill
Structured session traces with step metadata, sampled payloads, full capture on failure
Keep full logging and add full-text search and longer retention over the raw payloads

explanation: Correct: C. Observability at scale means structure and sampling: traces that link every step of a session, metadata you can query, and full payloads only for a sample plus the failures you need to debug. Why not the others: A removes the information needed to diagnose anything; B keeps the cost problem and loses history; D makes the cost problem bigger and still searches raw text rather than structured steps.

prompt: A hospital's ward-planning agent needs to book patient transfers with an ambulance company that runs its own dispatch agent. Each side insists that its internal systems and tools stay private. Which connection mechanism fits?

options.text: The hospital agent is given API credentials for the transport provider's booking system
The transport provider publishes an MCP server exposing its tools to the hospital agent
An agent-to-agent protocol: the agents exchange messages and keep their tools private
A third-party database that both organisations' agents read from and write to

explanation: Correct: C. When autonomous agents under different ownership must cooperate without exposing internals, agent-to-agent communication fits: each side keeps its tools behind its own agent and they exchange messages at the boundary. Why not the others: A and B expose one organisation's systems to the other's agent, which was ruled out; D couples both organisations to shared data more tightly than either would accept.

prompt: A claims-intake service in an insurer's existing pipeline must call Claude once per submitted form to label its claim type. The pipeline is deterministic, the service owns the whole flow, and no tool discovery is needed. Which integration mechanism is most appropriate?

options.text: A direct Claude API call from the service with the form and labelling instructions
An MCP server wrapping the claims service so that the model can discover and call it
An autonomous agent with the claims service's functions registered as its tools
An agent-to-agent exchange with a separate labelling agent run by another team

explanation: Correct: A. A single deterministic model call inside existing application code is a direct API integration; MCP and agents add discovery and autonomy this pipeline does not want. Why not the others: B inverts the direction, since the service calls the model rather than the model calling the service; C and D add planning and messaging overhead to a one-shot labelling step.

prompt: A RAG index is rebuilt nightly from a documentation site. After some rebuilds the assistant quotes superseded pages for part of the day. Which indexing practice addresses this most directly?

options.text: Rebuild the index hourly instead of nightly so superseded pages are replaced sooner
Build the new index fully, switch to it atomically, and version each chunk's metadata
Instruct the model to prefer whichever retrieved chunk sounds most recent if two conflict
Retrieve more chunks per query so the current version of a page is more likely included

explanation: Correct: B. Stale answers after a refresh come from serving a half-updated index or mixing old and new chunks; an atomic swap plus versioned metadata removes both causes. Why not the others: A makes the window of inconsistency more frequent rather than smaller; C asks the model to guess at freshness; D raises the chance of serving stale chunks alongside current ones.

prompt: An agent has three tools named `search_docs`, `find_docs` and `lookup_docs` with similar one-line descriptions, and it frequently picks the wrong one. What should the architect change first?

options.text: Merge the overlapping tools and give each a distinct name and clear usage guidance
Add a fourth tool whose only job is to decide which of the three search tools to call
Increase retries so the agent eventually lands on the right tool for each request
Present the three tools in random order each request to avoid bias toward the first

explanation: Correct: A. Tool selection is driven by names and descriptions; overlapping tools with vague one-liners are the root cause, so consolidate and describe precisely, including when not to use each. Why not the others: B adds indirection on top of the ambiguity; C makes errors slower and more expensive rather than rarer; D shuffles a problem it does not solve.

prompt: An internal MCP server exposes a `run_sql` tool that accepts arbitrary SQL against the analytics warehouse. The agent using it only ever needs monthly revenue by region. A security review asks for a change. Which is the best?

options.text: Keep `run_sql` and add a system-prompt rule that only SELECT statements may be issued
Replace `run_sql` with a narrow read-only tool such as `revenue_by_region(month)`
Keep `run_sql` and log every statement so misuse can be reviewed by security
Keep `run_sql` and have the model confirm each query with the user before running it

explanation: Correct: B. A tool's interface defines the blast radius: a narrow, parameterised, read-only tool gives the agent exactly the capability it needs and nothing else, and improves selection and reliability too. Why not the others: A puts a security boundary in the prompt; C only detects misuse after the fact; D pushes the control onto the user and slows every request.

prompt: A pharmaceutical company has built a regulatory-guidance repository that several agent teams, and teams not yet formed, will need to query. Each team currently writes its own integration. Which mechanism serves this best?

options.text: A direct API call coded into each agent that needs to read the repository
A shared system prompt that embeds the repository contents for every agent
An MCP server for the repository that any agent can connect to and discover
A nightly export of the repository sent to each team to load however it prefers

explanation: Correct: C. Exposing a capability once, with discoverable tools and resources, for any model application to use is what MCP is for; new teams connect without writing an integration. Why not the others: A repeats the integration work per agent; B does not scale and goes stale as the repository changes; D is a data hand-off rather than an integration and leaves each team to build its own.

prompt: A RAG assistant for a field-service company must answer two kinds of query: free-text questions about repair procedures, and lookups of a specific job by job number. Which TWO measures best match retrieval to these query patterns? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use a single vector index for both and rely on the model to notice when a match is wrong
Retrieve the top 100 chunks for every query so the right one is always in context
Remove job numbers from the index so they cannot confuse semantic search
Use semantic retrieval for procedure questions and exact-match lookup for job numbers
Attach equipment type and date metadata to chunks so retrieval filters before ranking

explanation: Correct: D and E. Different query patterns call for different retrieval paths, and metadata filtering narrows the candidate set before semantic ranking runs. Why not the others: A leaves the exact-identifier weakness in place and hopes the model compensates; B floods the context with noise; C deletes the data the lookup use case depends on.

prompt: An architect is reviewing the authentication design of an agent that calls several internal APIs on behalf of users. Which TWO findings represent security gaps? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Internal API keys sit in the system prompt so the model can include them in calls
The agent acts under one shared service identity regardless of which user is asking
Tool calls run in application code that holds credentials outside the model's context
Each tool call carries the end user's identity and the API enforces that user's rights
Credentials are rotated regularly and scoped to the minimum each tool needs

explanation: Correct: A and B. Secrets in the prompt can leak through output or injection, and a single shared identity means the API cannot enforce per-user permissions, leaving the model as the only access control. Why not the others: C keeps credentials out of the model, D propagates identity to the enforcing layer, and E applies least-privilege scoping; all three are correct practices, not gaps.

prompt: A legal-operations team is designing an agent and must decide whether tools and reference material are loaded on demand or placed in context up front. Which TWO characteristics most strongly favour loading on demand? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Every request uses the same three tools and a short prompt that rarely changes
The system must complete each request in exactly one model call with no lookups
The tool and reference set is large and any one request uses only a small part
New tools and documents arrive often and must be usable without a prompt redeploy
The whole context fits comfortably in the window and is covered by prompt caching

explanation: Correct: C and D. Progressive discovery pays off when the full set is large and sparsely used, and when the catalogue changes often, because on-demand loading keeps prompts small and lets new capabilities appear without prompt changes. Why not the others: A and E describe small, stable contexts where loading everything is simpler and cheaper; B rules out the extra lookup step that discovery needs.

prompt: A broadcaster's MCP server for its news archive must offer a publish action the model decides when to invoke, article texts the client attaches as context, and editorial templates journalists pick from a menu. How should these map onto MCP primitives?

options.text: All three as tools, since tools are the only primitive Claude clients consume
options.explanation: MCP also defines resources and prompts; forcing all into tools hands context and templates to the model.

options.text: Articles as prompts, templates as resources, and the publish action as a tool
options.explanation: This swaps two primitives: prompts are user-selected templates and resources are application-managed context.

options.text: Publish as a tool, articles as resources, and templates as prompts users choose
options.explanation: Correct: tools are model-controlled, resources are application-controlled, prompts are user-controlled.

options.text: Publish as a prompt so a journalist confirms it, with articles and templates as resources
options.explanation: Prompts are user-invoked templates, not an approval gate; confirming a write belongs in the client layer.

explanation: Correct: C. MCP defines three server primitives with different controllers: tools are model-controlled actions, resources are application-controlled context such as article texts, and prompts are user-controlled templates shown as menu items. Why not the others: A assumes tools are the only usable primitive; B swaps resources and prompts; D misuses prompts as an approval gate, which belongs in the client layer.

prompt: A SaaS vendor ships its MCP server as a local stdio package; each customer pastes a personal API key into a config file. The vendor now wants to update the server centrally and let users sign in with their existing vendor accounts instead of handling keys. Which design fits?

options.text: Keep the stdio package but embed one vendor-wide API key so users need no configuration
options.explanation: A shared embedded key gives every user identical, unrevocable access and still needs reinstalls for updates.

options.text: Keep the stdio package, add an auto-update check, and keep reading each user's API key
options.explanation: This eases updates but keeps users handling long-lived API keys, which the vendor wants to remove.

options.text: Host it remotely over Streamable HTTP with MCP's OAuth-based authorisation for sign-in
options.explanation: Correct: a remote server updates in one place, and MCP authorisation over HTTP uses OAuth so users sign in.

options.text: Host it remotely on an unauthenticated endpoint, with an unguessable URL per customer
options.explanation: An unguessable URL is a bearer secret with no user identity, scoping or revocation, and leaks easily.

explanation: Correct: C. A remote MCP server over the Streamable HTTP transport is updated centrally, and the MCP authorisation specification for HTTP transports builds on OAuth, so users sign in and the client gets a user-scoped token. Why not the others: A shares one unrevocable key and still needs reinstalls; B fixes updates but keeps users handling API keys; D replaces authentication with a bearer URL that leaks easily.

prompt: A logistics company's nightly reconciliation agent runs unattended. It authenticates with the stored refresh token of the operations manager who set it up, inheriting that manager's full finance and dispatch permissions. The manager leaves next month. What should change?

options.text: Re-authorise the agent with the successor's refresh token before the manager departs
options.explanation: This repeats the flaw: the agent still borrows a person's broad permissions and acts under a human's name.

options.text: Create one shared administrator account for every scheduled automation job
options.explanation: A shared admin identity maximises privilege and blast radius and makes jobs' actions indistinguishable.

options.text: Extend the manager's refresh token lifetime and keep it in the secrets manager
options.explanation: Keeping a departed employee's credential alive defeats offboarding and leaves an orphaned token in use.

options.text: Issue the agent its own workload identity, scoped only to what the nightly job needs
options.explanation: Correct: an unattended job should act as itself with least-privilege scopes that survive staff changes.

explanation: Correct: D. An agent that runs without a user should not borrow a person's delegated credentials; it needs its own workload identity scoped to the systems and operations the job uses, so actions are attributable and offboarding does not break it. Why not the others: A and C keep a human's broad permissions attached to the agent; B puts every job under one maximally privileged shared account.

prompt: A fintech's remote MCP server fronts its internal payments API. It forwards whatever OAuth access token the MCP client presents, unchanged, to the payments API without checking whom the token was issued for. A security review flags this. Which change addresses the finding?

options.text: Accept only tokens issued for the server itself, and use a separate scoped token upstream
options.explanation: Correct: audience validation plus a distinct downstream token removes the token passthrough MCP forbids.

options.text: Keep forwarding the client's token but require TLS between the server and the payments API
options.explanation: Encryption protects the token in transit but the server still relays tokens never meant for it.

options.text: Keep forwarding the client's token but shorten its lifetime to a few minutes
options.explanation: Short lifetimes reduce exposure but do not fix the missing audience check or confused-deputy risk.

options.text: Have the model pass a payments-API token in each tool call's arguments instead
options.explanation: Putting credentials in model-generated arguments exposes them to the model and to injection.

explanation: Correct: A. The MCP authorisation specification requires servers to validate that tokens were issued for them and forbids token passthrough; calls to an upstream API must use a separate token obtained for that API and scoped to what the server does. Why not the others: B and C harden the token without fixing the audience check or the confused-deputy risk; D moves the credential into the model's context.

prompt: A university's student-support agent only reads enrolments and grades from the records API. It uses a years-old API key with read and write access to every module, no expiry, and a home in a config file in the code repository. Which change most reduces the risk?

options.text: Replace the key with short-lived run-time tokens scoped to the read calls the tools make
options.explanation: Correct: narrow read-only scope and short expiry shrink what a leaked credential can do and for how long.

options.text: Move the existing key out of the repository into an environment variable on the server
options.explanation: Removing it from version control helps, but the credential is still long-lived and still has write access.

options.text: Keep the key and add a system-prompt rule that the agent must never call a write endpoint
options.explanation: A prompt rule is not an access control; injection or a model error can still reach allowed endpoints.

options.text: Rotate the same broad key yearly and alert whenever it is used outside office hours
options.explanation: Annual rotation and alerting detect some misuse but leave a year-long, over-privileged credential in place.

explanation: Correct: A. The key is over-scoped, long-lived and badly stored. Short-lived tokens issued at run time and scoped to read-only operations fix scope and lifetime at the enforcing layer, and remove the stored secret. Why not the others: B fixes only the storage; C relies on the prompt for authorisation; D adds detection but leaves the over-privileged long-lived key in use for another year.

prompt: A B2B retailer's account agent has a `list_orders` tool that returns every order for a customer as full JSON. For large trade customers that is thousands of orders, results get truncated, and the agent misses recent orders. How should the tool be redesigned?

options.text: Raise the tool-output token limit so the largest customer's full list fits in one response
options.explanation: This keeps flooding the context with mostly irrelevant rows, raising cost and diluting attention.

options.text: Summarise the full list with a second model call before returning it to the agent
options.explanation: A summary adds latency and cost and can drop the exact orders the agent needs.

options.text: Load each customer's whole order history into the system prompt at session start
options.explanation: This moves the same oversized payload into every request and goes stale during the session.

options.text: Add date and status filters, paginate with concise fields, and give a count and next page
options.explanation: Correct: filtering, pagination and concise defaults keep results relevant and tell the model how to get more.

explanation: Correct: D. Anthropic's tool-writing guidance recommends high-signal results: support filtering and pagination, choose sensible defaults, return concise fields unless detail is requested, and when output is truncated tell the model how to fetch more. Why not the others: A only enlarges the problem; B adds a lossy and slow extra step; C moves the oversized, changing data into the prompt on every request.

prompt: A city council's permit-booking agent calls a `book_inspection` tool. When the date is in the wrong format or the slot is already taken, the tool returns only `Error 400`. The agent then either repeats the identical call or tells the resident the system is down. What is the best fix?

options.text: Return an error saying what was wrong and how to fix it, such as the expected date format
options.explanation: Correct: specific, actionable error content lets the model fix its arguments or offer alternatives.

options.text: Wrap the tool in a retry loop that resends the identical request up to five times
options.explanation: Resending the same malformed or conflicting request cannot succeed; it only adds latency and load.

options.text: Suppress the error and return an empty success so the conversation carries on smoothly
options.explanation: Hiding the failure leads the model to believe the booking worked or to invent an outcome.

options.text: Return the full stack trace and the internal service logs so the model has maximum detail
options.explanation: Raw internals are noisy, can leak sensitive details, and still do not show what valid input looks like.

explanation: Correct: A. Anthropic's tool-writing guidance recommends error responses that clearly say what went wrong and how to correct it, and tool results can be flagged as errors so the model knows the call failed. Why not the others: B retries a request that cannot succeed; C hides the failure and invites fabrication; D floods the model with internals that do not help and may expose sensitive data.

prompt: An insurer's RAG assistant indexes 40 policy wordings chunked by section. Many chunks read like "The excess for this cover is 250 pounds" with no mention of their product, so home-insurance questions often retrieve the travel or motor policy's chunk. Which change addresses the cause?

options.text: Prepend a short header naming policy, product and section to each chunk before indexing
options.explanation: Correct: situating context added before embedding makes otherwise identical chunks distinguishable.

options.text: Split sections into single-sentence chunks so each embedding captures one precise fact
options.explanation: Smaller chunks strip away even more context, making chunks from different products harder to tell apart.

options.text: Raise the number of retrieved chunks from five to thirty so the right product is included
options.explanation: More results add noise and cost, and the model still cannot tell which look-alike chunk is which.

options.text: Tell the model to ignore any retrieved chunk that does not name the product asked about
options.explanation: The relevant chunks lack the product name themselves, so this would discard the right answer too.

explanation: Correct: A. Once cut from their document the chunks lose the context that distinguishes them. Contextual retrieval prepends chunk-specific context, such as the document and section it comes from, before embedding, which sharply reduces retrieval failures. Why not the others: B removes more context; C widens recall without making chunks distinguishable; D filters on a signal the correct chunks do not contain.

prompt: An HR-advice SaaS indexes employment-law guidance for twelve countries, superseded versions included. A German user asking about current notice periods often gets similar Austrian guidance or last year's version. The user's country is known. Which retrieval change fits best?

options.text: Append "for Germany, current rules" to every query before embedding it
options.explanation: Query wording nudges similarity but cannot reliably exclude another country or an old version.

options.text: Train a separate embedding model for each country so German guidance is embedded apart
options.explanation: Per-country models are costly to maintain and still do nothing to exclude superseded versions.

options.text: Store country and effective dates as chunk metadata and filter retrieval on both
options.explanation: Correct: hard metadata filters exclude the wrong jurisdiction and superseded versions before ranking.

options.text: Increase the overlap between neighbouring chunks so each carries more surrounding text
options.explanation: Overlap helps with split sentences but does not stop similar content elsewhere outranking the right chunk.

explanation: Correct: C. The query carries structured attributes (country, and the need for current rules) that semantic similarity alone cannot enforce. Storing jurisdiction and effective dates as chunk metadata and filtering on them restricts the candidate set before ranking. Why not the others: A only nudges the query vector; B is expensive and ignores versioning; D addresses boundary splits, not jurisdiction or currency.

prompt: A media group moved its RAG pipeline to a new embedding model with better multilingual support. New articles and all queries now use the new model, but the archive still holds vectors from the old one, and archive retrieval has become close to random. What should the team do?

options.text: Normalise all vectors to unit length so scores from the two models become comparable
options.explanation: Normalisation fixes scale, not meaning; vectors from different models live in unrelated spaces.

options.text: Embed each query with the old model as well, then merge both result lists into one ranking
options.explanation: This doubles the work, merges scores from incomparable spaces, and keeps the weaker model in service.

options.text: Re-embed the whole archive with the new model into a new index, validate it, then switch
options.explanation: Correct: queries and documents must share one embedding model, so a model change needs a full re-index.

options.text: Keep the archive vectors and add a re-ranking step to correct for the model mismatch
options.explanation: A re-ranker only reorders the candidates it receives, and the mismatched first stage is not surfacing them.

explanation: Correct: C. Embeddings from different models occupy different vector spaces, so a query vector from the new model cannot be compared with archive vectors from the old one; changing model means re-embedding the corpus, validated before cut-over. Why not the others: A changes vector length, not the space; B merges incomparable scores and keeps both models; D cannot recover candidates the first stage never retrieves.

prompt: A freight forwarder's analysts ask "how many shipments to Rotterdam arrived late last quarter, by carrier?". Each shipments-table row was embedded as a text chunk and the assistant retrieves the top 20. Its counts are consistently wrong. What should the architect do?

options.text: Give the agent a parameterised query tool over the shipments database for aggregates
options.explanation: Correct: counts and group-bys over structured rows are database queries, which return exact results.

options.text: Use larger chunks that each hold hundreds of rows so more shipments fit in the top 20
options.explanation: Bigger chunks still return a similarity-ranked sample, so totals remain incomplete.

options.text: Raise the retrieved chunk count above the number of shipments in a typical quarter
options.explanation: This floods the context with rows and still relies on the model to count thousands of items.

options.text: Switch to the largest available model so it reasons more carefully over the rows
options.explanation: The model is counting an incomplete sample; a stronger model cannot recover rows retrieval never returned.

explanation: Correct: A. Aggregation over a structured table needs exact filtering and grouping, which a database query does natively; vector retrieval returns a similarity-ranked sample of rows, so any count built from it is incomplete. Why not the others: B and C keep the wrong mechanism and only change the sample size; D blames the model for rows that retrieval never supplied.

prompt: A platform team's Claude Code agents run in sandboxed CI containers and must check deployment status and roll back releases. A mature deployment CLI is already installed there, and only this team needs it. An engineer proposes an MCP server wrapping all 40 CLI commands. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Run the CLI from the agents' shell tool, allow-listing subcommands and scoping credentials
options.explanation: Correct: for one team's sandboxed agents, a mature CLI is a direct, low-cost interface once scoped.

options.text: Build an MCP server with one tool per CLI command so all 40 operations become discoverable
options.explanation: A one-to-one wrapper adds a service to maintain and 40 definitions to context for a single consumer.

options.text: Paste the CLI's full reference manual into every session's system prompt up front
options.explanation: Loading the whole manual every run wastes context; the agent can read help output when needed.

options.text: Stand up a separate deployment agent reached through an agent-to-agent protocol
options.explanation: Agent-to-agent suits independently owned agents; here one team owns everything and a tool call suffices.

explanation: Correct: A. When sandboxed agents already have a shell and a mature CLI exists, using it directly is often the simplest integration once subcommands are allow-listed and credentials scoped; MCP pays off when many clients share it. Why not the others: B builds a wrapper for one consumer and adds tool bloat; C spends context on a whole manual every run; D adds agent-to-agent coordination with no separate owner.

prompt: A travel agency's booking agent calls a partner airline's API, which returns HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header at peak times. The tool retries immediately in a tight loop, the model sometimes re-issues the call too, and duplicate bookings appear after busy periods. Which design addresses this?

options.text: Add a system-prompt instruction to wait several seconds before re-issuing a throttled call
options.explanation: The model cannot reliably pause or coordinate timing, and the tool's own retry loop continues regardless.

options.text: Honour Retry-After with capped jittered backoff in the tool layer and use idempotency keys
options.explanation: Correct: backoff in code respects the limit and idempotency keys make repeated bookings safe.

options.text: Keep retrying immediately but fire several identical requests in parallel to get through
options.explanation: Parallel retries amplify the overload, worsen throttling and multiply duplicate bookings.

options.text: Ask the airline for a higher rate limit and remove all retry logic from the tool
options.explanation: A higher limit may help capacity but peaks still throttle, and duplicates remain possible without idempotency.

explanation: Correct: B. Rate-limit handling belongs in deterministic code: respect Retry-After, back off with capped jitter, make non-idempotent operations such as bookings safe to repeat with idempotency keys, and return a clear result when retries run out so the model does not loop. Why not the others: A leaves timing to the model; C makes the overload worse; D treats capacity as the only issue and ignores duplicate writes.

prompt: A research system's orchestrator delegates to three subagents, each calling MCP servers on different hosts. Every component logs with its own request IDs, so engineers spend hours matching timestamps to reconstruct one session during incidents. Which change fixes this most directly?

options.text: Synchronise every host's clock precisely so that all events can be correlated by timestamp
options.explanation: Accurate clocks help ordering but cannot tell which concurrent session an event belonged to.

options.text: Have each subagent write a natural-language summary of its work to a shared log
options.explanation: Self-reported summaries omit failing steps and timing and are not linked to the underlying calls.

options.text: Create a per-session trace ID, propagate it through every call, and record steps as spans
options.explanation: Correct: one propagated trace context ties every step across hosts into a single queryable tree.

options.text: Ship all component logs to one central store with full-text search on the user's ID
options.explanation: Centralising helps, but a user ID spans many sessions and does not link parent and child steps.

explanation: Correct: C. Distributed tracing gives each session one trace ID propagated across process and host boundaries, and records each orchestrator step, subagent run, tool call and MCP request as a span with a parent link, so one trace shows the whole tree. Why not the others: A and D improve log handling but cannot separate concurrent sessions or show causality; B relies on agents reporting their own failures.

prompt: A grocer's product assistant has an accuracy target of 88% and a p95 latency budget of 2.5 s; differences under one point are noise. Config 1 (top-5): 86%, 1.3 s. Config 2 (top-10): 90%, 1.6 s. Config 3 (top-10, extended thinking): 91%, 3.8 s. Config 4 (top-20): 90.5%, 2.2 s. Which decision is best justified?

options.text: Config 3, as the most accurate, and ask stakeholders to relax the latency budget
options.explanation: Its one-point gain is within noise and it breaches the agreed latency budget by a wide margin.

options.text: Config 1, as the fastest and cheapest, accepting a small shortfall on the accuracy target
options.explanation: It misses the agreed accuracy target, so it fails a stated requirement.

options.text: Config 2, which clears both targets with margin, noting why configs 3 and 4 were rejected
options.explanation: Correct: it meets both targets; the alternatives break the budget or pay for a within-noise gain.

options.text: Config 4, as the most accurate option that still fits inside the latency budget
options.explanation: Its half-point edge over config 2 is within noise, while costing latency headroom and more tokens.

explanation: Correct: C. A justified decision meets the agreed targets and does not pay for differences the evaluation cannot distinguish; config 2 clears 88% with margin at 1.6 s, and recording rejected options keeps it reviewable. Why not the others: A breaks the latency budget for a within-noise gain; B fails the accuracy target outright; D treats a half-point, within-noise difference as real while spending headroom.

prompt: A consultancy's agent connects to nine MCP servers exposing about 250 tools. Definitions take a large share of each request's context and selection mistakes are rising. Most requests use three or four tools; a few are used in nearly every session. Which TWO measures best address this? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Merge all 250 tools into one generic `call_tool` that takes a name and free-form arguments
options.explanation: This hides every tool's purpose and parameters, making selection and argument construction harder.

options.text: Enable tool search so most definitions are deferred and loaded only when searched for
options.explanation: Correct: deferred loading keeps rarely used definitions out of context until a request needs them.

options.text: Move to a model with a larger context window so all 250 definitions fit comfortably
options.explanation: More room does not reduce the token cost or the confusion caused by hundreds of similar tools.

options.text: Shorten every tool description to a single line so each definition uses minimal tokens
options.explanation: Terse descriptions save tokens but make tools harder to tell apart, worsening selection.

options.text: Keep the handful of tools used in nearly every session loaded rather than deferring them
options.explanation: Correct: always-needed tools should stay loaded so common requests avoid an extra search step.

explanation: Correct: B and E. Tool search lets definitions be marked for deferred loading so the model discovers them on demand, cutting context use and aiding selection; the docs recommend keeping the most frequently used tools non-deferred so common requests stay fast. Why not the others: A destroys the information the model needs to choose; C pays for the same bloat with more context; D trades selection accuracy for tokens.

prompt: A customer-service SaaS runs one Claude agent for 300 tenants, each with its own knowledge base and prompt config. One tenant's answer quality degraded for two weeks before it complained; platform-wide dashboards showed nothing. Which TWO strategies would have caught this sooner? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Store every prompt, response and retrieved document so any tenant session can be replayed
options.explanation: Capturing everything is costly and does not by itself raise an alert when one tenant degrades.

options.text: Track platform-wide average latency, token spend and error rate on a daily dashboard
options.explanation: Platform averages are exactly what hid the problem; one tenant out of 300 barely moves them.

options.text: Have an engineer read ten random conversations from across the platform each week
options.explanation: Ten random conversations a week rarely include the affected tenant and give no trend.

options.text: Tag every trace and metric with tenant ID and config version so quality can be sliced
options.explanation: Correct: per-tenant and per-version dimensions let a confined regression show instead of averaging away.

options.text: Score a sample of each tenant's traffic with an automated evaluator and alert on drops
options.explanation: Correct: continuous sampled quality scoring detects degradation that latency and error metrics miss.

explanation: Correct: D and E. At multi-tenant scale a local regression disappears in global averages, so traces and metrics need tenant and configuration-version dimensions, and quality itself must be measured continuously by scoring sampled traffic per tenant and alerting on drops. Why not the others: A is expensive and passive; B is the averaged view that missed the problem; C samples far too little to find one tenant's issue.

prompt: A chemicals manufacturer is designing RAG over safety procedures with numbered steps and tables of exposure limits. Operators usually ask about one step, but answers are only safe when the surrounding steps and limits are included. Which TWO design choices fit best? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use fixed 100-token chunks with no overlap to maximise precision on a specific step
options.explanation: Tiny fixed chunks split steps and tables and hand the model fragments without their safety context.

options.text: Embed each complete procedure manual as a single vector so no context is separated
options.explanation: One vector per long manual blurs many topics together, so matching a specific step becomes unreliable.

options.text: Index step-level chunks for matching but pass the whole enclosing procedure to the model
options.explanation: Correct: small units match precisely while the parent section keeps adjacent steps and limits together.

options.text: Strip the tables out before indexing because embedding models handle tabular text poorly
options.explanation: Removing the exposure-limit tables throws away information the answers must include.

options.text: Retrieve a wider candidate set, then re-rank it and keep only the most relevant few
options.explanation: Correct: a re-ranking stage improves which candidates reach the model without reducing first-stage recall.

explanation: Correct: C and E. Matching on small units while returning the larger parent section (small-to-big retrieval) gives precise hits without losing the surrounding steps and limits that safety answers depend on, and retrieving broadly then re-ranking improves the precision of what reaches the model. Why not the others: A fragments procedures; B makes step-level matching unreliable; D deletes the tables operators need.

prompt: For a new expense-claims agent, the team must choose between looking up tools and policy text per request and carrying all of it in a fixed prompt. Which TWO characteristics most strongly favour carrying everything up front? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The agent spans many business domains with hundreds of tools, each used by few requests
options.explanation: A large, rarely used catalogue is the classic case for on-demand discovery.

options.text: The reference material is large and parts of it change hourly as upstream systems publish
options.explanation: Large, fast-changing material bloats every request and keeps invalidating any cached prefix.

options.text: The toolset is small and stable, most requests use nearly all of it, and the prefix caches
options.explanation: Correct: when nearly everything is needed every time and the prefix is cacheable, up-front loading is cheap.

options.text: A strict latency budget rules out an extra discovery round-trip, and the full context fits
options.explanation: Correct: if everything fits and latency is tight, avoiding a search or fetch turn is worth the tokens.

options.text: Requests vary widely and each needs a different small subset of the tools and documents
options.explanation: Varied requests that each touch a small subset are what progressive discovery is designed for.

explanation: Correct: C and D. Monolithic context wins when the material is small, stable and needed on almost every request, so caching makes the prefix cheap, and when an extra discovery round-trip would break a latency budget the full context fits in. Why not the others: A and E describe large or varied needs that progressive discovery serves better; B describes content too volatile to load and cache on every request.

prompt: A legal-research assistant retrieves 20 chunks of about 800 tokens per query, re-ranks them, and passes all 20 to the model. Its p95 latency is 4.2 seconds against a 3-second target, and evaluation shows answers almost always draw on the five top-ranked chunks. Which change best restores the target?

options.text: Move all queries to a smaller, faster model and accept whatever accuracy results
Drop the re-ranking stage and pass all 20 raw retrieval results straight on to the model
Keep retrieving 20, re-rank, pass only the top five, and check accuracy on the eval set
Cut chunks to 200 tokens and keep passing all 20 so the context shrinks fourfold

explanation: Correct: C. The evidence shows the model uses only the top five re-ranked chunks, so sending fewer input tokens cuts latency and cost where the time is actually spent, and the eval set confirms accuracy is unchanged. Why not the others: A trades accuracy blindly for speed; B removes the stage that puts the right chunks first and saves little; D rewrites the index and risks the fragment problems that cost accuracy.

prompt: A data-migration agent runs sessions of 80 or more tool calls. Each call returns a large JSON result that stays in the conversation, so later turns approach the context limit, cost climbs, and the agent starts repeating earlier mistakes. Which context strategy best addresses this?

options.text: Move to the model with the largest context window so the whole history always fits in
Compact older tool results into a short state summary and refetch details when needed
Drop the system prompt from later turns so the growing history has more room
Truncate every tool result to its first 200 characters as soon as it is returned

explanation: Correct: B. Long agent sessions need active context management: replace used tool results with a compact record of what was learned and keep a way to fetch details again, so the window holds current state rather than stale payloads. Why not the others: A delays the limit and still degrades attention over a bloated history; C removes the instructions that govern behaviour; D destroys data before the agent has used it.

prompt: A procurement assistant sends a 6,000-token policy document and definitions for 70 tools on every request. Input cost per request is high and time-to-first-token is slow, yet most requests use fewer than five tools. Which TWO changes most reduce input cost without hurting quality? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Put the policy document and tool definitions first in the prompt and cache that prefix
Shorten the policy document by deleting the sections that only cover unusual edge cases
Switch to a model with a larger context window so the full prompt processes faster
Defer rarely used tool definitions so they load only when the model searches for them
Lower the output token limit so each response ends sooner and costs less

explanation: Correct: A and D. The stable policy and tool block is identical on every request, so placing it first and caching the prefix cuts repeated input cost and latency; deferring rarely used definitions keeps dozens of unused tools out of context. Why not the others: B removes guidance the assistant may need; C adds capacity without reducing the tokens sent each request; E limits output, which is not where the cost lies.

prompt: A city council has piloted an assistant that answers residents' building-permit questions. Councillors want to know if it can go live; so far the evidence is a handful of positive comments from residents. What should the architect put in place first?

options.text: Extend the pilot to more residents so there are more comments to present to councillors
A dashboard of the token spend and latency the platform already emits
The offline evaluation suite the platform team uses for its other assistants
Agreed metrics for accuracy, latency, cost and safety, with launch thresholds

explanation: Correct: D. "Good enough" has to be defined before it can be measured: agree the metrics and the thresholds that count as ready, then measure the assistant against them. Why not the others: A only collects more anecdotes; B measures what is easy to emit rather than what matters, and omits accuracy and safety; C borrows another system's suite before this one's targets exist.

prompt: An airline's rebooking assistant goes live next quarter. The quality lead is choosing the conversations the release will be judged on. Which set should be chosen?

options.text: Synthetic conversations generated and then graded by the assistant's own model
The twenty conversations from the sales demo deck, since stakeholders will try those first
Real anonymised conversations plus adversarial edge cases, each with a reference answer
Whatever pilot users typed in the first week, graded only by thumbs-up counts

explanation: Correct: C. A trustworthy set reflects real traffic, includes the hard and adversarial cases that break systems, and carries reference answers so grading is consistent. Why not the others: A measures the model against itself on data it generated; B is a tiny, flattering sample; D has no ground truth, so a confident wrong answer and a right one score the same.

prompt: A cosmetics brand's copywriting assistant produces about 5,000 product blurbs a week, and the brand team needs to know whether they sound on-brand. Only a few can be read by a person. Which evaluation method fits?

options.text: A model-as-judge grader using a written rubric, calibrated on a human-labelled sample
Exact string matching of each output against a bank of approved reference copy
A weekly hand review of ten random outputs by the brand team, with no automated checks
Tracking average output length, since on-brand copy tends to fall in a consistent range

explanation: Correct: A. Tone and brand are subjective qualities that string matching cannot measure; a rubric-driven model grader scales to thousands of outputs, provided it is calibrated against human judgements and monitored for drift. Why not the others: B fails on any valid rewording; C covers a fraction of a percent of output and misses systematic problems; D measures a proxy with no real relation to tone.

prompt: A support chatbot's new prompt scores five points higher than the live one on the team's offline test set. Before switching every customer over, the product owner wants more confidence. What is the right next step?

options.text: Replace the production prompt now, because the offline suite is the agreed quality gate
Survey the pilot users on which of the two prompts they prefer before deciding
Re-run the offline suite until the gap is statistically convincing, then deploy
Run an A/B test on a fraction of live traffic and compare the agreed metrics first

explanation: Correct: D. Offline gains do not always hold on live traffic; an A/B test on real requests with pre-agreed metrics confirms the gain with a small blast radius if it does not hold. Why not the others: A skips the live check entirely; B measures preference on a tiny sample rather than the agreed metrics; C only tightens an offline estimate of the same distribution.

prompt: An e-commerce company runs six Claude workloads, from product tagging to fraud-case summaries, and the board wants the monthly model bill down by 40%. An engineer suggests moving all six to the cheapest model tier this week. What should the architect do before agreeing?

options.text: Agree, since the target is a business decision and the smallest model reaches it fastest
Refuse, since model downgrades tend to lower quality and should not be entertained
Profile the spend per workload, then test cheaper options against the evaluation suite
Switch only the costliest workload to the smallest model and wait for complaints

explanation: Correct: C. Cost optimisation starts by measuring where the tokens go, then applies the cheapest change that holds quality, verified by evaluation; the smallest model may suit some workloads and not others. Why not the others: A and D change production without measuring quality; B rejects a reasonable goal instead of finding the safe route to it.

prompt: A newly released model version promises better reasoning, and a logistics company wants its routing assistant on it. A developer tried twenty requests by hand and saw no problems. How should the switch be made?

options.text: Switch all traffic at once during a quiet period so any problems surface at low volume
Run the evaluation suite on the new version, then ramp up gradually with rollback ready
Keep the old version indefinitely, since a system that is working should not be changed
Switch only the staging environment and leave production on the old version until asked

explanation: Correct: B. A model change is a change to system behaviour: evaluate it against the suite, then expose it gradually with monitoring and a rollback path. Why not the others: A makes the whole user base the test; C ignores deprecation and forgoes improvements; D never completes the migration and gains no evidence about production behaviour.

prompt: A legal research tool answers lawyers' questions from a case-law index. The architect wants to know that answer quality is slipping before the lawyers notice it. Which signal gives the earliest warning?

options.text: The number of support tickets mentioning the tool, reviewed at the end of each month
Total monthly token spend compared with the budget approved for the tool
The uptime percentage of the retrieval service and the vector database behind it
Retrieval quality on sampled live queries: relevance scores and unsupported-answer rate

explanation: Correct: D. In a RAG system quality usually breaks at retrieval first, so monitoring relevance and unsupported answers on a live sample shows degradation before it reaches users. Why not the others: A is a lagging indicator by definition; B tracks cost, not quality; C says the service is up, not that it returns the right chunks.

prompt: A summarisation feature using a small, fast model produces accurate summaries of short emails but consistently drops key points from 50-page reports, even with a well-structured prompt. Which system issue is this?

options.text: A hallucination, since the summaries contain content the source reports do not
A prompt failure, since the instructions about completeness are not being followed
A retrieval failure, since the wrong parts of the long reports are being fetched
A model mismatch, since the model copes with the short task but not the long one

explanation: Correct: D. The same prompt works on easy inputs and fails on hard ones, which points to the model's capability on long, dense documents rather than the prompt; the fix is a more capable model or decomposition. Why not the others: A describes invented content, but the problem here is omission; B is unlikely when the identical prompt succeeds on short inputs; C does not apply, as there is no retrieval step.

prompt: A parcel-tracking assistant invents a plausible tracking number when the lookup tool returns no result, instead of telling the customer that nothing was found. What is the issue and the most direct fix?

options.text: A hallucination; specify the empty-result behaviour and check numbers against tool output
A model mismatch; move to a larger model that will know the correct tracking numbers
A retrieval failure; index more parcels so the lookup tool returns a result more often
A latency issue; the tool is timing out and the model fills the gap, so raise the timeout

explanation: Correct: A. Fabricating a value to fill a gap is a hallucination; the fix is to specify the empty-result behaviour in the prompt and to check output values against what the tool actually returned. Why not the others: B fails because no model knows tracking numbers it was not given; C misreads a correct empty result as a failure; D invents a cause the scenario does not describe.

prompt: An assistant told to "answer in two sentences" keeps producing long answers. Inspection of the system prompt finds a later section that says "explain your reasoning fully". Which issue is this?

options.text: A model mismatch, since a more capable model would reconcile the two instructions
A prompt failure from conflicting instructions; remove one and state the intent once
A hallucination, since the model is generating content the user did not ask for
A context-window problem, since the prompt is too long for the model to attend to fully

explanation: Correct: B. Two instructions that cannot both be satisfied are a prompt defect; the model is simply following one of them, and the author should remove the conflict. Why not the others: A asks a model to resolve an ambiguity the author should remove; C is wrong because the content is relevant, just too long; D is not indicated by anything in the scenario, as the prompt is short.

prompt: A document-analysis pipeline's p95 latency is 9 seconds. Tracing shows three sequential model calls of about 2.5 seconds each plus a 1.5-second retrieval step, and the second and third calls do not depend on each other. Which optimisation gives the largest latency reduction without changing quality?

options.text: Run the second and third calls in parallel, removing one call from the critical path
Enable prompt caching on all three calls so that each of them returns almost instantly
Move all three calls to the smallest model to roughly halve the time taken by each
Remove the retrieval step and rely on the model's own knowledge of the documents

explanation: Correct: A. The trace shows two independent calls running in sequence; running them in parallel removes a whole 2.5-second call from the critical path with no change to outputs. Why not the others: B cuts time-to-first-token on cached prefixes but does not remove generation time; C changes quality, which the question rules out; D removes grounding and will change answers.

prompt: A nightly job classifies 300,000 documents. Results are needed by the next morning and nobody waits on an individual document. Which change most reduces cost without changing the model or the prompt?

options.text: Run the requests through the synchronous API with higher concurrency to finish sooner
Shorten every document to its first paragraph before classification to cut input tokens
Retry each request several times and keep the cheapest response that comes back
Submit the documents through the batch API, trading unneeded latency for a lower price

explanation: Correct: D. Batch processing is the designed trade: asynchronous completion within a window in exchange for a lower price, which fits a nightly job with no interactive user. Why not the others: A finishes faster but does not cost less; B changes the inputs and therefore the results; C makes no sense, since pricing is per token and retries only add cost.

prompt: A pharmaceutical company's assistant will answer medical-information questions from doctors, and the regulator will inspect how it was tested. Which TWO elements belong in the pre-launch test plan? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A demo script showing the assistant's best answers to executives and the regulator
A held-out test set with reference answers that the prompt was never tuned against
Adversarial cases probing injection, policy violations and safety limits, expert-graded
A single aggregate quality score so results are simple to communicate to leadership
An evaluation run only on the final day before launch so it reflects the shipped version

explanation: Correct: B and C. A regulated setting needs a clean held-out set with reference answers, so scores are not inflated by tuning, plus adversarial cases graded by people who know the domain, showing that the boundaries hold under attack. Why not the others: A is marketing, not evaluation; D hides the per-category failures a regulator will ask about; E leaves no time to act on the findings.

prompt: Over the last two weeks, an online retailer's returns assistant has slowly started giving worse answers. Nobody has touched its prompts, the model version is pinned, and response times are flat. Which TWO places should the team look first? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Traces of failing sessions showing which chunks were retrieved and tools called
The total number of requests per day over the two weeks, broken down by hour and channel
User satisfaction survey results collected at the end of each of the two weeks
The model provider's public status page and incident history for the two-week period
The mix of live inputs over the period, checked for new query types or languages

explanation: Correct: A and E. With model, prompt and latency ruled out, what changed is what flows through the system: traces show what the model was given in failing cases, and the input mix shows whether traffic has drifted from what the system was designed for. Why not the others: B is volume and cannot explain a quality change; C confirms the symptom without locating the cause; D matters for outages, not gradual degradation.

prompt: A team wants to reduce token usage on a long-running support conversation without harming answer quality. Which TWO techniques apply? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Omit the system prompt after the first turn, since the model retains it across the session
Summarise older turns past a length threshold, keeping the facts the assistant still needs
Raise `max_tokens` on every turn so the model can restate the history it needs itself
Truncate every tool result to its first line as soon as it is returned to the model
Prune large tool results from earlier turns once used, leaving a short note of the finding

explanation: Correct: B and E. Context management for long sessions means compacting history and clearing bulky tool outputs once they have served their purpose, while preserving the facts still needed. Why not the others: A breaks the assistant, because each request is stateless and the system prompt must be sent every time; C adds output tokens rather than removing input tokens; D destroys information before it has been used.

prompt: A freight forwarder uses Claude to extract the HS code, declared value, currency and country of origin from customs invoices into a fixed JSON schema. The team has 400 invoices whose correct field values were already keyed in by brokers. Which grading method fits this evaluation best?

options.text: Code-based grading that parses each output and compares every field with the broker values
options.explanation: Right: the expected values are known and exact, so a deterministic comparison is fast, cheap and reproducible.

options.text: A model-graded rubric asking a second model to rate each extraction on a 1-to-5 scale
options.explanation: A judge model adds cost and variance where an exact comparison against known values is possible.

options.text: Human review of every extraction by customs specialists, marking each as acceptable or not
options.explanation: Slow and expensive for a task with known answers; humans are better spent on ambiguous outputs.

options.text: Semantic similarity between the output and the broker record, scored by an embedding model
options.explanation: Similarity blurs exact values; a wrong HS code or currency can still look very close to the right one.

explanation: Correct: A. When the task has an objectively correct answer that is already known, code-based grading (parse the JSON, compare each field exactly) is the fastest, most reliable and most scalable method, and it reports accuracy per field. Why not the others: B adds a judge's variance and cost for no gain; C spends expert time on a check a script can do; D treats a wrong digit in an HS code as nearly correct.

prompt: A news publisher compares two headline prompts with a pairwise model judge that sees both headlines and names the better one. Prompt X's headline is always shown first and wins 71% of comparisons, yet editors reviewing a sample see little difference. What should the architect change first?

options.text: Switch the judge to a larger model, which is less swayed by superficial features
options.explanation: Larger judges still show position bias; the fixed ordering must be removed in the test design.

options.text: Ask the judge for a score per headline instead of a preference, then average per variant
options.explanation: Can help, but leaves the confound untested; first check whether order alone drives the result.

options.text: Present every pair in both orders and count a win only when the judge agrees with itself
options.explanation: Right: swapping order exposes and neutralises position bias; inconsistent verdicts count as ties.

options.text: Keep the setup but run ten times as many comparisons so the 71% becomes robust
options.explanation: More samples make a biased estimate more precise, not more correct; the order effect persists.

explanation: Correct: C. Model judges are known to favour a response because of its position, so always placing X first confounds the comparison. Running each pair in both orders and counting only consistent preferences removes the bias and shows how often the judge merely follows order. Why not the others: A assumes size cures the bias; B changes the format without testing the confound; D makes a biased number look more certain.

prompt: An airline's refund agent acts without human review, so a scenario that passes once and fails the next time is unacceptable. Each of 120 test scenarios was run once and 92% passed, but repeated runs at production temperature vary. Which metric best reflects the reliability needed?

options.text: pass@k: the share of scenarios in which at least one of k repeated runs succeeds
options.explanation: pass@k rewards getting it right once in k tries, which suits pick-the-best workflows, not unattended actions.

options.text: The single-run pass rate re-measured at temperature zero, so each run is identical
options.explanation: Lower temperature reduces but does not remove variation, and it measures a configuration unlike production.

options.text: The mean pass rate over k runs per scenario, so occasional failures average out
options.explanation: An average hides which scenarios are flaky; a 90% mean can come from many scenarios failing one run in ten.

options.text: The share of scenarios where all k runs pass, with a list of the inconsistent ones
options.explanation: Right: requiring every trial to pass (often called pass^k) measures the consistency unattended actions demand.

explanation: Correct: D. For an agent acting unattended, reliability means succeeding every time, so the right metric counts scenarios where all k trials pass and lists the flaky ones for diagnosis. Why not the others: A (pass@k) measures the chance of at least one success and rises with k, the wrong direction; B evaluates a different configuration and may still vary; C averages away the inconsistency that matters.

prompt: At a SaaS company, five engineers edit the system prompts of a billing assistant. Twice this quarter a small wording change fixed one complaint but broke invoice-dispute handling, which was only noticed by customers. How should the team prevent this?

options.text: Version the prompts and gate every change on a per-category regression suite run in CI
options.explanation: Right: prompts are code; automated per-category checks in CI catch a dispute regression before release.

options.text: Require a senior engineer to approve each prompt diff and judge its effect on other topics
options.explanation: Review helps, but people cannot reliably predict how wording shifts behaviour on other topics.

options.text: Freeze the system prompt and handle new complaints with post-processing rules in the app
options.explanation: Avoids prompt regressions by blocking improvement and accumulating brittle patches; no safety net.

options.text: Run a monthly evaluation of production and roll back if the overall score has dropped
options.explanation: Monthly and aggregate: customers meet the regression first, and an overall score can hide one category.

explanation: Correct: A. Treating prompts like code, with versioning and a regression suite that runs on every change and enforces thresholds per category, including invoice disputes, catches side effects before customers see them. Why not the others: B relies on human prediction of model behaviour; C stops iteration instead of protecting it; D detects problems late and can hide a category-specific drop in an aggregate.

prompt: A travel agency's booking agent is graded by comparing its tool calls with a recorded reference sequence. Many failed runs produced the correct booking by a different valid route, and a few passing runs issued an unnecessary cancellation. How should the evaluation be redesigned?

options.text: Loosen the matcher so a run passes when 80% of its tool calls appear in the reference run
options.explanation: Still ties grading to one path and would keep passing runs that made a harmful extra cancellation.

options.text: Record several reference sequences per scenario and pass a run matching any one exactly
options.explanation: Valid routes keep multiplying; this stays brittle and still ignores whether forbidden actions occurred.

options.text: Grade the end state of the booking system and check each transcript for forbidden actions
options.explanation: Right: outcome grading accepts any valid route, while transcript checks catch harmful steps.

options.text: Drop automated grading and have travel consultants judge if each transcript is sensible
options.explanation: Human review helps calibration, but it does not scale to regression runs and is less consistent.

explanation: Correct: C. Agents can reach the right result by many legitimate paths, so grading the outcome avoids penalising valid variation, while explicit transcript checks catch steps that must never happen, such as an unrequested cancellation. Why not the others: A and B keep grading tied to particular paths and miss harmful actions; D is too slow and inconsistent to be the main regression method.

prompt: A law firm's RAG assistant over case files scores 74% on end-to-end answer correctness, down from 85% after a re-indexing project. Engineers disagree on whether retrieval or generation is at fault. Which evaluation change settles the question fastest?

options.text: Rerun the suite with a larger model; if the score recovers, generation was the weak stage
options.explanation: A stronger model can partly compensate for poor retrieval, so this would not separate the stages.

options.text: Measure recall@k on labelled passages and, separately, whether each answer is grounded
options.explanation: Right: stage-level metrics show whether the right passages are retrieved and whether answers stay faithful.

options.text: Ask lawyers to rate a sample of answers for usefulness to get a richer quality signal
options.explanation: A richer end-to-end rating is still end-to-end; it does not show which stage causes the drop.

options.text: Instruct the model to cite its sources, then compare the answer score before and after
options.explanation: Changes the system instead of diagnosing it; any score movement still mixes both stages.

explanation: Correct: B. Retrieval and generation need separate metrics: recall@k on labelled relevant passages shows whether re-indexing broke retrieval, and groundedness shows whether the model is using what it was given. Why not the others: A and C remain end-to-end and confound the two stages; D is a fix applied before the cause is known, and its effect also mixes both stages.

prompt: A university's student-services assistant runs an A/B test of a new prompt. After two days and about 150 rated conversations per arm, the new prompt has 81% positive ratings against 78% for the current one. The product owner wants to switch everyone over today. What should the architect advise?

options.text: Switch now, since a three-point gain in ratings is meaningful for a student-facing service
options.explanation: With about 150 ratings per arm, a three-point gap is well within the noise; the gain may not be real.

options.text: Switch now but keep the old prompt available so it can be restored if complaints rise
options.explanation: Rollback is useful, but this still decides on a difference the data cannot distinguish from chance.

options.text: Estimate the sample size needed to detect a gain this size and keep the test running to it
options.explanation: Right: deciding the required sample in advance and reaching it is what makes the comparison trustworthy.

options.text: Stop the test and rely on the offline suite, since user ratings are too subjective to use
options.explanation: User ratings are a valid online signal; the problem is sample size, not the kind of metric.

explanation: Correct: C. A three-point difference on roughly 150 ratings per arm has a wide confidence interval and is easily produced by chance or day-of-week effects, so the team should work out the sample needed to detect a gain of that size and run until it is reached. Why not the others: A and B act on noise; D discards a legitimate online signal instead of collecting enough of it.

prompt: A health insurer tightened the safety instructions of its member assistant after it once gave risky advice about combining medicines. The harmful-response rate on the red-team set fell to near zero. Which measurement should accompany that result before the change is judged a success?

options.text: The false-refusal rate on legitimate but sensitive member questions about their coverage
options.explanation: Right: over-tightening shows up as refusals of benign questions, which only a benign-sensitive set reveals.

options.text: The harmful-response rate on a second, larger red-team set, to rule out a sampling fluke
options.explanation: Useful for confidence, but it measures the same side of the trade-off and cannot reveal over-refusal.

options.text: Average response length before and after the change, since safer answers tend to be short
options.explanation: Length is a weak proxy; it says nothing direct about whether legitimate questions are now declined.

options.text: The latency and token cost of the longer system prompt, to confirm it is affordable
options.explanation: Worth tracking, but cost is not the main risk created by stricter safety instructions.

explanation: Correct: A. Safety guardrails trade two error types: harmful completions and false refusals. A near-zero harmful rate is only a success if members with legitimate sensitive questions are still answered, so a benign-but-sensitive set with a false-refusal metric must be measured alongside it. Why not the others: B re-measures the same side of the trade-off; C is an indirect proxy; D tracks a secondary concern.

prompt: A wealth-management firm's research agent reads third-party filings and web pages and can send emails and create tasks. The security team wants each new release to be assessed for prompt-injection resistance in a way that is comparable from release to release. What should the evaluation include?

options.text: A one-off penetration test by an external firm before launch, added to the release notes
options.explanation: Valuable, but a one-off test does not give a repeatable measure for each subsequent release.

options.text: A versioned injection set hidden in documents and tool results, scored by actions taken
options.explanation: Right: a fixed, growing attack suite with an objective criterion gives a comparable attack-success rate.

options.text: Direct user requests to ignore instructions, graded on whether the agent declines
options.explanation: Covers only direct injection; the main risk here is indirect injection through content the agent reads.

options.text: A model judge over production responses that flags any which seem influenced by injection
options.explanation: Monitoring helps in production, but appearance-based judging is not a controlled, repeatable test.

explanation: Correct: B. A red-team suite of injection payloads embedded where the agent actually meets untrusted text, graded on whether a forbidden email or task is actually produced, yields an attack-success rate that is comparable across releases and can grow as new attacks appear. Why not the others: A is not repeatable; C ignores indirect injection, the main risk here; D is monitoring, not a controlled evaluation.

prompt: A telecom's chat assistant takes about six seconds to produce a typical answer, and the interface shows a spinner until the full response arrives. Abandonment analysis shows most users leave within the first three seconds. Which change most improves the experience without changing the model?

options.text: Switch to the Batch API so requests are processed more efficiently and cost less each
options.explanation: Batch processing is asynchronous and suits offline workloads; it would make interactive answers slower.

options.text: Stream the response so text appears while it is generated, tracking time to first token
options.explanation: Right: streaming cuts perceived wait to the time to first token, which is when users are abandoning.

options.text: Raise `max_tokens` so answers are never cut off, avoiding follow-ups that add waiting
