options.explanation: A higher limit does not speed up generation and does nothing for the initial wait that drives abandonment.

options.text: Show a progress bar based on average latency so users see how long the answer will take
options.explanation: A better spinner still makes users wait six seconds for any content to appear.

explanation: Correct: B. Users are abandoning before any answer appears, so the metric that matters is time to first token, not total latency. Streaming shows text within a fraction of the total generation time, and tracking TTFT separately shows whether the improvement holds. Why not the others: A suits offline jobs, not live chat; C does not affect speed; D only decorates the wait.

prompt: A council's permit assistant has a short system prompt and short questions, yet answers average 700 output tokens: they restate the question, add a preamble and end with a summary. Traces show generation dominates latency and cost. Which change best reduces both while protecting quality?

options.text: Cache the system prompt, since cached prefixes are cheaper and faster on every request
options.explanation: Caching reduces input cost and time, but here the input is small and the output dominates.

options.text: Set `max_tokens` to 250 so the model cannot produce the long answers that drive the cost
options.explanation: A hard cap truncates answers mid-sentence instead of making them concise; it fails users.

options.text: Move to a larger model, which follows instructions more closely and writes shorter answers
options.explanation: A larger model is usually slower and costlier per token; the verbosity comes from the output spec.

options.text: Specify a concise format without restatement or summary, and confirm quality on the evals
options.explanation: Right: removing redundant output cuts the dominant cost and latency, and the eval run guards substance.

explanation: Correct: D. Output tokens drive both latency and cost here, and much of the output is redundant, so tightening the answer specification (no restated question, preamble or repeated summary) directly reduces them; rerunning the evaluation confirms quality is preserved. Why not the others: A optimises input, which is already small; B truncates rather than condenses; C typically raises per-token cost and latency.

prompt: A manufacturer uses Claude to turn inspection reports into a JSON list of defects. About 3% of responses fail to parse, almost all from the longest reports, each ending partway through an object. The longest reports use a small fraction of the context window. What should the engineer check first?

options.text: Whether the prompt's example JSON has a syntax error the model copies into some outputs
options.explanation: A copied error would appear across report sizes and at the same place, not as cut-off endings.

options.text: The `stop_reason` of the failing responses, to see whether they hit the `max_tokens` limit
options.explanation: Right: endings cut off mid-object on the longest inputs point to truncation, which the stop reason confirms.

options.text: Whether the model invents defects in long reports, producing malformed entries when unsure
options.explanation: Hallucinated content would usually still be well-formed JSON; it does not explain abrupt stops.

options.text: Whether long reports exceed the context window, so the model loses the schema instructions
options.explanation: Reports are far smaller than the window, and that limit would surface as an error or a different stop reason.

explanation: Correct: B. Responses ending mid-object, concentrated on the longest inputs, are the signature of output truncation; the API reports `stop_reason: max_tokens` in that case, and the fix is a higher limit or a split output. Why not the others: A would not track input length or end abruptly; C would usually still produce valid JSON; D is implausible at this size and would surface as a different stop reason or an error.

prompt: A recruitment platform tuned its CV-screening prompt over 40 iterations, each time checking the same 60 test CVs and fixing any that failed. The prompt now scores 98% on that set, yet recruiters say live shortlists are no better than before. What is the likely cause and the right response?

options.text: The model is too small for screening; move to a larger model and repeat the tuning loop
options.explanation: Nothing points to model capacity; repeating the same tuning loop would reproduce the same problem.

options.text: Recruiters distrust the system; show them the 98% score and test cases to build confidence
options.explanation: Dismisses real field evidence; a gap between test and live results is a signal to investigate.

options.text: Live vacancies differ from the test set; swap the 60 CVs for 60 new ones and keep tuning
options.explanation: Swapping one small tuning set for another repeats the overfitting unless a separate held-out set is kept.

options.text: The prompt overfits the test set; hold out a larger set of live CVs used only to measure
options.explanation: Right: tuning repeatedly on one small set fits its quirks; only untouched data measures real performance.

explanation: Correct: D. Iterating many times on the same 60 cases and patching each failure fits the prompt to that set's quirks, so its score stops predicting live performance. The remedy is a larger, representative held-out set drawn from live vacancies and used only for measurement. Why not the others: A assumes a capacity problem with no evidence; B ignores the signal; C repeats the same mistake on new data.

prompt: A logistics company has agreed a service-level objective that 95% of its dispatch assistant's responses complete within four seconds. The assistant performs retrieval, two tool calls and one model call per request. Which TWO monitoring practices best support this objective? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Alert whenever any single request exceeds four seconds so on-call sees every slow response
options.explanation: The objective allows 5% of requests to be slower; per-request alerts create noise and alert fatigue.

options.text: Report daily average response time to operations, with a red flag above four seconds
options.explanation: An average can stay under four seconds while the slowest tail breaches the objective; daily is too slow.

options.text: Log the full prompt and response of every request so slow ones can be replayed in reviews
options.explanation: Full payloads help some investigations but do not measure latency or show which step is slow.

options.text: Alert when rolling p95 latency approaches four seconds, before the objective is breached
options.explanation: Right: alerting on the percentile the objective is defined on, with headroom, gives early warning.

options.text: Record per-step timings for retrieval, each tool call and the model call on one trace ID
options.explanation: Right: step-level spans show which stage is pushing the tail up, turning an alert into a diagnosis.

explanation: Correct: D and E. The objective is defined on the 95th percentile, so alerting on rolling p95 with headroom warns before a breach, and per-step spans linked by a trace ID show whether retrieval, a tool or the model is responsible. Why not the others: A alerts on requests the objective already allows to be slow; B hides the tail behind an average; C stores content but does not measure or localise latency.

prompt: An insurer scores claim-file summaries with a model judge told to "rate this summary from 1 to 10 for quality". The judge's scores rise with summary length, and claims handlers often disagree with its rankings. Which TWO changes most improve the judge's reliability? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Replace the single score with a rubric of specific, levelled criteria like omitted facts
options.explanation: Right: specific, anchored criteria give the judge something concrete to check instead of rewarding length.

options.text: Widen the scale from 1-to-10 to 1-to-100 so the judge can express finer differences
options.explanation: A finer scale adds false precision; it does not address the vague criterion or the length bias.

options.text: Make the model and prompt that wrote the summaries the judge, since it knows the intent
options.explanation: Self-grading invites self-preference and shares the generator's blind spots.

options.text: Score a sample claims handlers have also graded, and track the judge's agreement with them
options.explanation: Right: calibrating against expert labels shows whether the judge can be trusted and whether changes help.

options.text: Tell the judge to give its score immediately without any explanation, to keep grading fast
options.explanation: Asking for reasoning before the score usually improves judge quality; suppressing it hurts reliability.

explanation: Correct: A and D. A vague "quality" score lets superficial features such as length drive the result, so a rubric with specific, anchored criteria focuses the judge on what matters, and checking agreement with claims handlers' grades shows whether the judge is trustworthy. Why not the others: B adds false precision; C introduces self-preference; E removes the reasoning step that tends to make judgements more reliable.

prompt: An online retailer wants to A/B test a new product-question prompt on live traffic before replacing the current one. Which TWO design choices are most important for the result to be trustworthy? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Randomly assign users to a variant and keep each user on that variant for the whole test
options.explanation: Right: random, sticky assignment removes selection bias and stops users seeing both variants.

options.text: Run the new prompt this week and compare its metrics with last week's on the old prompt
options.explanation: Sequential comparison confounds the prompt with seasonality, promotions and other changes.

options.text: Let customers opt in to the new assistant from a banner, so only willing users are exposed
options.explanation: Self-selected users differ systematically from the rest, so differences cannot be attributed to the prompt.

options.text: Send the new prompt only to the smallest regional storefront so any harm is limited
options.explanation: Limits risk but gives a small, unrepresentative sample whose results may not generalise.

options.text: Fix the primary and guardrail metrics, such as escalation rate and cost, before starting
options.explanation: Right: pre-registering metrics prevents picking whichever number looks good and catches side effects.

explanation: Correct: A and E. Random, sticky assignment makes the two groups comparable, and fixing the primary and guardrail metrics in advance stops after-the-fact metric shopping while watching for side effects such as more escalations or higher cost. Why not the others: B confounds the change with time; C introduces self-selection bias; D trades representativeness for safety and may not generalise.

prompt: A contract assistant answers questions over documents of 50 to 300 pages. It scores 94% on the test set, yet lawyers report missed clauses in the longest files. Every test question targets a clause near the start of its document. How should the evaluation change?

options.text: Raise the pass threshold from 94% to 98% so that the remaining errors are forced out
Add questions whose answers sit in the middle and at the end of the longest documents
Shorten each contract to its first 50 pages so the test matches the model's strong range
Switch to a model with a larger context window and re-run the existing test set

explanation: Correct: B. The test set only probes the start of each document, so it cannot see the failure lawyers report: information deep in long inputs being missed. Answers placed at varied depths make the suite measure the behaviour that matters. Why not the others: A raises the bar on a set blind to the problem; C hides the failing range instead of testing it; D changes the system before the suite can measure the effect.

prompt: A facilities agent can draft tenant notices, update maintenance tickets and book contractors for jobs costing up to 25,000 euros. Management wants human oversight that does not slow routine work. Where should the approval gate sit?

options.text: In front of every single action, so that nothing happens until a person approves
Nowhere, because the 25,000 euro ceiling on contractor jobs is already a control
After each booking, in a weekly review of the jobs the agent has placed
Before costly or hard-to-undo actions such as bookings; drafts and tickets flow

explanation: Correct: D. A human gate belongs where an action is costly or hard to reverse, such as committing money to a contractor; low-risk, reversible steps like drafting and ticket updates can run unattended. Why not the others: A removes the efficiency the agent was meant to bring; B mistakes a spending ceiling for oversight; C reviews bookings after the cost has already been committed.

prompt: A Spanish telecom's support assistant forwards full chat transcripts, including customer names and phone numbers, to a sentiment-analysis vendor in the United States. The data protection officer objects under GDPR. Which architectural change best answers the objection?

options.text: Update the privacy notice to state that transcripts may be analysed by a vendor abroad
Keep exporting full transcripts but encrypt them in transit and at rest
Pseudonymise before export, send only the fields needed, use a lawful transfer basis
Stop sentiment analysis so no customer data ever leaves the telecom's systems

explanation: Correct: C. The objection is that more personal data leaves the EU than the purpose needs, so the fix is data minimisation in the pipeline: pseudonymise or strip identifiers before export, send only what the analysis needs, and cover the transfer lawfully. Why not the others: A is notice, not a safeguard; B protects the channel but still exports personal data; D removes a needed capability rather than fixing it.

prompt: A pharmacy chain wants an assistant that answers pharmacists' questions from customers' prescription histories. Which consideration must be settled at the architecture stage rather than deferred to a later release?

options.text: The chunk size and overlap used when indexing the prescription records
How protected health information flows end to end, with access control and audit
Which model tier the first release should use for answering pharmacists
The exact wording of the disclaimer pharmacists see when they first open the tool

explanation: Correct: B. Regulated data flows are structural: which services touch protected health information, where it is stored, who can access it and how it is audited determine what the architecture may be, and cannot be retrofitted once the data has flowed. Why not the others: A is tunable after launch without rebuilding; C can change from release to release; D is a presentation detail that can be edited at any time.

prompt: A scholarship-screening assistant rates applicants from certain secondary schools systematically lower, even though names, gender and ethnicity were stripped from its input. What does this most likely indicate, and what should be done?

options.text: The model is malfunctioning; redeploy it and re-run every affected application
The stripped fields were not the issue; restore them so the model has full context
A proxy such as school encodes a protected trait; audit inputs and test by group
The pattern is coincidence; take no action until more applications are collected

explanation: Correct: C. Removing explicit demographic fields does not remove bias when other inputs stand in for them; a school can track ethnicity or income. The response is to find the proxies, measure outcomes by group and make fairness tests a standing part of evaluation. Why not the others: A treats a data problem as an outage; B reintroduces the direct attributes; D ignores a systematic disparity with legal consequences.

prompt: A penetration test of a contract-review assistant shows that text inside an uploaded contract can steer it: a hidden instruction asking it to disclose its system prompt partly succeeded. What is the correct architectural response?

options.text: Treat document text as untrusted data: delimit it and enforce the real limits in code
Add a prompt line telling the model to ignore document instructions, then close the issue
Scan uploads for the phrase "ignore previous instructions" and reject any that contain it
Stop accepting uploaded contracts and answer only from the model's training knowledge

explanation: Correct: A. Indirect prompt injection is a trust-boundary problem: content from outside the system is data, not instructions, and the limits on what the assistant can reveal or do must hold in code whatever the model is persuaded to say. Why not the others: B relies on the prompt alone, which the test already showed is not enough; C blocks one phrasing of an unbounded set; D removes the product's core capability.

prompt: A utility company is putting a Claude-powered chat window on its billing page. Its compliance officer asks what in the design meets the duty to be open with customers about the AI. Which measure addresses this most directly?

options.text: Tuning replies to sound as human as possible so customers feel at ease
Keeping the system prompt confidential so that rivals cannot copy the assistant's tone
Choosing the largest available model so answers are correct more often
Disclosing that the customer is talking to an AI, its limits, and a route to a human

explanation: Correct: D. Transparency in deployment means customers know they are dealing with an AI, understand what it can and cannot do, and can reach a person when the matter is consequential; that is what regulators and ethics guidance ask for. Why not the others: A works against transparency by hiding the AI's nature; B is confidentiality, a different concern; C is about accuracy, a separate obligation.

prompt: A customer-service assistant must never include a customer's full card number in any reply, regardless of what the customer or a retrieved document says. Which control is the primary one?

options.text: A system-prompt instruction asking the model to be careful with card numbers
A human review of every single reply before it is sent, regardless of its content
A monthly audit of a random sample of sent replies, checking each for leaked card numbers
A deterministic filter outside the model that detects and redacts card-number patterns

explanation: Correct: D. An absolute never rule on a pattern that can be detected deterministically belongs in an output guardrail enforced in code; it holds even when the model has been manipulated by a user or a document. Why not the others: A is a soft control that an injection can override; B works but is disproportionate for a rule a pattern match enforces; C finds leaks a month after customers saw them.

prompt: A lending assistant produces loan-approval recommendations, each of which has significant financial and regulatory consequences. Which control should be primary?

options.text: An output filter that blocks any recommendation containing certain high-risk phrasings
A dashboard of approval and rejection rates over time, reviewed by the risk team
A human decision-maker who reviews and owns each recommendation before it takes effect
A fuller system prompt describing the lending policy and all of its exceptions

explanation: Correct: C. For high-stakes, regulated decisions the primary control is human validation: the model recommends and an accountable person decides, so no consequential outcome rests on the model alone. Why not the others: A catches surface wording, not bad judgement; B is monitoring, which reveals trends only after decisions have taken effect; D improves the input but leaves the model as the decision-maker.

prompt: Compliance must be able to show, months after the event, exactly what an agent did and why during a disputed transaction. Which control provides this?

options.text: A human approval step before each transaction, recorded in the approval tool
An output filter applied to every reply the agent sends to the customer in the transaction
A gateway rate limit on how many transactions the agent can process per hour
An immutable, timestamped audit log of each step, tool call, input and decision

explanation: Correct: D. Reconstructing a past decision needs a complete, tamper-evident record of what the agent saw, called and decided, retained for as long as regulation requires. Why not the others: A prevents some bad actions but records only the approval, not the agent's reasoning; B shapes output rather than recording it; C limits volume and says nothing about any individual transaction.

prompt: A government agency wants to use a Claude-based assistant for internal case work and asks whether the deployment can meet FedRAMP requirements. What is the architect's correct first step?

options.text: Verify the platform is FedRAMP-authorised and keep agency data inside that boundary
Add a disclaimer saying the assistant must not be used for sensitive case data
Assume any cloud deployment is acceptable because the provider is a well-known company
Run the model on employees' laptops so the agency avoids cloud compliance obligations

explanation: Correct: A. FedRAMP compliance is a property of the authorised environment, not of the model: the architect must verify that the platform used carries the authorisation and keep the agency's data within that boundary. Why not the others: B changes nothing about where the data goes; C substitutes reputation for authorisation; D is not feasible for a hosted model and does not remove the obligations.

prompt: A product owner proposes that a Claude assistant give final answers on medication dosages to patients with no clinician involved, because "the model is very accurate". Which limitation of LLM systems most directly argues against this design?

options.text: LLMs cannot do the arithmetic that dosage calculations need reliably enough
LLM latency is too high for a patient-facing channel such as this one
LLMs can be fluently, confidently wrong, so high-harm uses need a human check
LLMs cannot be used in healthcare under current regulation, so the design is unlawful

explanation: Correct: C. The decisive failure mode is confident error: fluency is not accuracy, and where a wrong answer can cause serious harm the design needs human validation before the answer reaches the patient. Why not the others: A is not decisive, since arithmetic can be checked in code; B is manageable and not a safety argument; D overstates the position, since healthcare use is possible with appropriate controls.

prompt: A water utility's assistant drafts replies to billing disputes. The regulator requires that no incorrect refund or credit promise ever reaches a customer. Which TWO controls most directly meet this requirement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A system prompt asking the model to be careful and accurate about refunds and credits
Human review and sign-off of every drafted reply before it is sent to the customer
A larger model, which makes fewer factual mistakes when it drafts the replies
A deterministic check that flags amounts and promises for the reviewer to verify
A faster response-time target so customers get answers to their disputes sooner

explanation: Correct: B and D. A requirement that none may reach the customer calls for hard controls: an accountable person signs off each outgoing reply, and an automated check surfaces every amount and promise so the reviewer verifies it against the account. Why not the others: A and C lower the error rate but cannot guarantee zero; E is about speed and does nothing for accuracy.

prompt: An agent reads inbound support tickets and can update CRM records. A security review flags that ticket text is attacker-controlled and could carry prompt injection. Which TWO measures most reduce the risk? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Ask the model to rate how trustworthy each ticket seems before deciding whether to act
Batch more tickets per run so any injected text is diluted by legitimate content
Limit the agent to the CRM fields the task needs and require confirmation for writes
Disable logging of ticket text so that injected content is never stored in traces
Delimit ticket text and tell the model it is data that may contain adversarial text

explanation: Correct: C and E. Defence in depth against injection combines limiting what a hijacked agent can do, through least-privilege tools and confirmation on consequential writes, with making the trust boundary explicit so the model treats ticket text as data. Why not the others: A asks the model to police itself; B adds more untrusted text rather than less; D hampers investigation and prevents nothing.

prompt: A team is listing the risks of a new customer-facing assistant for a risk register. Which TWO are genuine LLM-system failure modes that belong on the register? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The model fabricates a policy clause that does not exist in the source documents
The model refuses to run without an internet connection on the user's own device
Answer wording varies between identical requests, which some users notice and remark on
A crafted user input makes the assistant drop its scope and leak internal information
The model learns from each conversation and changes its own weights overnight

explanation: Correct: A and D. Hallucinated content and prompt injection are two central failure modes of LLM systems, and each needs an owner and a mitigation on the register. Why not the others: B describes a hosted service in a confused way rather than a failure; C is ordinary sampling variance, not a risk; E is false, because inference does not update the model's weights.

prompt: An employee-support assistant logs every prompt and reply in full to an observability platform most engineers can query. Employees often mention health conditions and salaries. Privacy wants this fixed without losing the ability to debug and audit. Which change best addresses the concern?

options.text: Turn off prompt and reply logging entirely and keep only latency and error-rate metrics
options.explanation: This removes the data but also the traces needed to debug, evaluate and audit the assistant.

options.text: Redact personal data before traces are stored; restrict any raw copy and expire it fast
options.explanation: Redacting before persistence keeps traces useful while limiting who sees personal data and for how long.

options.text: Instruct the assistant never to repeat health or salary details back to employees
options.explanation: The employee's own message is still logged in full, and the instruction is a soft control on output only.

options.text: Enable encryption at rest on the platform's storage volumes and rotate the keys regularly
options.explanation: Encryption at rest protects against stolen disks, not against the engineers who can query the logs.

explanation: Correct: B. Personal data is persisted in a widely accessible store, so the control belongs in the logging pipeline: redact or tokenise before storage and keep any unredacted copy access-restricted with short retention. Why not the others: A discards needed observability; C only shapes replies and leaves the employee's input logged in full; D addresses a different threat, as query users still see everything.

prompt: A European learning platform uses Claude to give feedback on essays. Essays are chunked into a vector store, conversations are kept in logs, and common answers sit in a semantic cache. A former student submits a GDPR erasure request. Which approach best supports honouring it?

options.text: Map the student's id to every store holding their data, then delete and verify in each one
options.explanation: Erasure has to reach every derived copy, which needs records traceable to the person across stores.

options.text: Delete the account and essays from the main database, as embeddings are not personal data
options.explanation: Embeddings and their stored chunk text can still relate to an identifiable person.

options.text: Ask the model provider to erase the essays from the model, since it generated the feedback
options.explanation: The essays live in the platform's own stores, not in the model, so this targets the wrong place.

options.text: Let cache and logs expire under their ninety-day retention; delete only the vector entries
options.explanation: Waiting for routine expiry does not honour a specific request, and logs still hold personal data.

explanation: Correct: A. In RAG, personal data is copied into derived stores (chunks and embeddings, logs, caches), so erasure needs a data map tying those copies to the person, then deletion and verification in each store. Why not the others: B wrongly treats embeddings and chunks as non-personal; C misplaces the data, which sits in the platform, not the model; D relies on routine expiry instead of acting on the request.

prompt: An insurer uses Claude to triage around 20,000 low-value travel claims a day. Policy requires that a person makes every claim denial. Most claims are straightforward approvals, and the operations team cannot staff review of every decision. Which human-review design fits best?

options.text: Review a random five per cent of decisions daily and use the error rate to tune the prompt
options.explanation: Random sampling alone lets most denials go out without a person deciding them.

options.text: Route all denials and high-value or uncertain cases to review; sample routine approvals
options.explanation: Mandatory review where policy or risk demands it, plus sampling elsewhere, meets the rule at manageable cost.

options.text: Require a reviewer to approve every decision and hire temporary staff for peak seasons
options.explanation: Full review satisfies the rule but is disproportionate for routine approvals the team cannot staff.

options.text: Have the model rate its confidence and auto-finalise any decision it rates above 0.9
options.explanation: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, and auto-finalising denials breaks the policy.

explanation: Correct: B. Human review should be risk-based: mandatory where policy or impact requires it (every denial, high value, uncertain cases) and sampled elsewhere so quality keeps being measured. Why not the others: A lets most denials go out without a person deciding them; C meets the rule at a staffing cost the scenario rules out; D relies on uncalibrated self-ratings and lets the model finalise denials, against policy.

prompt: A benefits agency has caseworkers approve Claude-drafted eligibility decisions. After six months, 99.6% of drafts are accepted unchanged with a median review time of nine seconds, and an appeal reveals approved drafts that misread income documents. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Treat the high acceptance rate as proof of accuracy and cut review back to a sample
options.explanation: High agreement with short review times signals rubber-stamping, and the appeal shows errors slip through.

options.text: Show a confidence score beside each draft so caseworkers can skim the confident ones
options.explanation: Showing confidence deepens anchoring on the model, and the misread drafts may well have looked confident.

options.text: Seed known-error cases, show source evidence beside key fields, and require confirmation
options.explanation: This counters automation bias by making reviewers check evidence and measuring whether review catches errors.

options.text: Add caseworkers to the review team so each has more time to spend on every draft decision
options.explanation: More time alone does not change the habit of accepting drafts, and nothing measures whether review improves.

explanation: Correct: C. Near-total acceptance in seconds, with missed errors, is a sign of automation bias: the human gate exists only on paper. Seeding known errors measures whether review works, and source evidence with required confirmation makes the check real. Why not the others: A misreads rubber-stamping as accuracy; B strengthens anchoring on the model; D adds capacity without changing behaviour or measuring it.

prompt: An asset manager's research assistant answers analysts' questions about company filings. Analysts report that when they push back ("Are you sure? I thought margins rose"), the assistant often abandons a correct answer and agrees with them. What should the architect do?

options.text: Set temperature to zero so the assistant gives the same answer every time it is asked
options.explanation: Lower temperature reduces sampling variation but does not stop the model deferring to pushback.

options.text: Ground answers in cited extracts, revise only on new evidence, add pushback turns to evals
options.explanation: This targets sycophancy directly: evidence anchors the answer and the eval measures whether it holds.

options.text: Move to the largest model available, since capable models do not cave to incorrect users
options.explanation: Capability may help, but assuming the problem away without grounding or measurement is not a control.

options.text: Disable follow-up messages so each question is answered in a single turn with no challenge
options.explanation: This removes a legitimate workflow, and analysts can still rephrase leading questions in a new turn.

explanation: Correct: B. Abandoning a correct answer under social pressure is sycophancy, a known LLM failure mode. Grounding claims in cited sources, changing the answer only on new evidence, and testing pushback turns in evals address it and make it measurable. Why not the others: A confuses sycophancy with non-determinism; C assumes the problem away without evidence; D breaks the product and does not remove leading questions.

prompt: An accounting firm builds an assistant that answers staff questions about tax thresholds and filing deadlines. The rules change every year, and some changed after the model's training data was collected. Which design best addresses this limitation?

options.text: Tell the model in its prompt that its tax knowledge is current and to answer confidently
options.explanation: Telling the model it is current does not give it the new rules and makes confident wrong answers likelier.

options.text: Pick the newest model release, since its training data will include this year's figures
options.explanation: Any model has a knowledge cutoff, and rules can change after it, so recency of release is not a control.

options.text: Retrieve the rule from a maintained source, cite its effective date, flag if none exists
options.explanation: Retrieval supplies post-cutoff facts, and dated citations let staff verify which rules the answer relies on.

options.text: Ask staff to prefix every question with "use the latest rules" so the model prefers them
options.explanation: The model cannot prefer rules it does not know, so the phrase changes nothing about its knowledge.

explanation: Correct: C. A model's knowledge stops at its training cutoff, so time-sensitive facts must be supplied at run time from a maintained source, cited with effective dates, with an explicit statement when nothing current is found. Why not the others: A and D only change wording and make confident errors more likely; B ignores that every model has a cutoff and that rules keep changing after it.

prompt: A media company's chatbot checks each user message with a moderation classifier before it reaches Claude. A red team shows that by escalating gradually over fifteen individually harmless turns, they can steer the bot into content the policy forbids. Which change best closes this gap?

options.text: Extend the per-message classifier with a longer blocklist drawn from the red-team logs
options.explanation: Each message looks harmless on its own, so a bigger keyword list on single messages misses the attack.

options.text: Cap conversations at three turns and force a new session so attackers cannot build context
options.explanation: This damages normal use and still allows attacks that fit in a few turns or span sessions.

options.text: Strengthen the system prompt with firm refusal rules and a reminder to stay within policy
options.explanation: Prompt instructions help but are a soft layer, and the red team has shown the model can be steered.

options.text: Screen outputs and the whole conversation, not single messages, and test multi-turn cases
options.explanation: Conversation-level and output checks catch harm that only emerges across turns; tests catch regressions.

explanation: Correct: D. Multi-turn jailbreaks exploit checks that look at one message at a time, so guardrails need to evaluate the accumulated conversation and screen what the model actually produces, with multi-turn cases kept in the red-team suite. Why not the others: A still looks at single messages; B is a blunt restriction that hurts users and is easily worked around; C is a useful layer but not sufficient on its own.

prompt: A SaaS analytics product lets Claude write and run Python against CSV files that customers upload, so users can ask questions about their own data. Uploaded files may contain text crafted to manipulate the model. Where should the generated code run?

options.text: In the main application server, after Claude reviews its own code for malice
options.explanation: Self-review by the same model that may have been manipulated is not an isolation boundary.

options.text: In the main server process, behind a blocklist on imports such as os, socket or subprocess
options.explanation: Import blocklists are easy to bypass, and the code would still share the server's secrets and network.

options.text: In an ephemeral sandbox per session: no secrets, no other tenants' data, limited egress
options.explanation: Isolation contains whatever the code does, even if the model was manipulated into writing something harmful.

options.text: In one long-lived shared container per region for fast start-up, with every script logged
options.explanation: Sharing a container across tenants risks cross-tenant leakage, and logging only detects problems afterwards.

explanation: Correct: C. Model-generated code is untrusted, since inputs may carry injected instructions, so it belongs in an isolated, ephemeral environment with no credentials, no cross-tenant access and limited egress. Why not the others: A relies on the possibly hijacked model to police itself; B is a bypassable filter inside a privileged process; D shares state between tenants and only detects issues later.

prompt: A retailer releases a new system prompt and model version for its shopping assistant to all users at once. Within an hour the assistant starts offering discount codes it is not authorised to give. Looking ahead, which capability would most limit the damage from a release like this?

options.text: A longer system prompt listing every case in which the assistant must not offer a discount
options.explanation: Better prompts may prevent this case but do nothing to contain the next unexpected regression.

options.text: Versioned prompt and model settings, a staged rollout with monitoring, and a kill switch
options.explanation: Staged rollout limits exposure, and a fast revert or tool kill switch stops harm without a full redeploy.

options.text: A weekly manual review of sample conversations so the team can raise anomalies at planning
options.explanation: Weekly review finds the problem days later, long after the unauthorised discounts went out.

options.text: A rule that every rollback goes through the full code-review and build pipeline first
options.explanation: Requiring the full pipeline for a rollback slows containment exactly when speed matters most.

explanation: Correct: B. Prompt and model changes alter behaviour as much as code changes, so they should be versioned, rolled out gradually with monitoring, and be instantly revertible, with the ability to disable a risky tool on its own. Why not the others: A addresses one symptom only; C detects the problem days too late; D makes rollback slow at the moment it needs to be immediate.

prompt: A small-business lender uses Claude to help underwriters assess loan applications. When an application is declined, the applicant must be told the specific main reasons, and those reasons must reflect what actually drove the decision. How should the system be designed?

options.text: After a decline, ask Claude to explain its reasons and forward that text to the applicant
options.explanation: A post-hoc explanation may be a plausible rationalisation rather than what drove the decision.

options.text: Enable extended thinking and forward the model's reasoning text to declined applicants
options.explanation: Raw reasoning text is not an applicant explanation and is not assured to reflect the true basis.

options.text: Send declined applicants a standard letter citing a range of factors the lender assessed
options.explanation: A generic statement does not give the specific reasons the lender is required to provide.

options.text: Score policy criteria as structured fields with linked evidence; derive reasons from them
options.explanation: Reasons drawn from the recorded criteria that drove the decision are specific, faithful and auditable.

explanation: Correct: D. For adverse decisions the explanation must match the actual basis, so the decision should rest on recorded criteria with linked evidence, and the reasons generated from those fields for an underwriter to confirm. Why not the others: A invites a post-hoc rationalisation; B treats reasoning text as a faithful, applicant-ready explanation, which it is not; C fails the requirement for specific reasons.

prompt: A US health-technology company plans to send patient intake notes containing protected health information (PHI) to the Claude API to produce clinician summaries. Which TWO steps should be settled before any PHI is sent? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Confirm a business associate agreement with the provider that covers every feature in use
options.explanation: HIPAA requires a BAA with vendors handling PHI, and coverage can depend on which features are used.

options.text: Rely on TLS to the API, since encrypting data in transit is all HIPAA asks of a vendor
options.explanation: Encryption in transit is one safeguard, not a substitute for a BAA and the other HIPAA requirements.

options.text: Send only the fields the summary needs and hold the firm's own PHI logs to HIPAA controls
options.explanation: Minimising PHI and securing the company's own copies covers the parts of the system it is responsible for.

options.text: Instruct Claude in the system prompt not to retain any patient data after summarising
options.explanation: Data retention is governed by the provider's terms and infrastructure, not by an instruction to the model.

options.text: Assume no agreement is needed because the provider does not train on API inputs by default
options.explanation: Not training on inputs does not remove the need for a BAA when a vendor processes PHI.

explanation: Correct: A and C. Sending PHI to a vendor requires a BAA that covers the services actually used, and the company must minimise the PHI it sends and protect its own copies in logs, traces and caches. Why not the others: B treats one technical safeguard as the whole requirement; D confuses model behaviour with provider data handling; E mistakes a training policy for a contractual agreement covering PHI processing.

prompt: An education company is launching a Claude-based homework tutor for pupils aged 11 to 16. The safeguarding lead wants layered guardrails rather than reliance on the model alone. Which TWO controls are correctly placed? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Screen pupils' messages on the way in only, as clean inputs guarantee acceptable replies
options.explanation: Harmless inputs can still produce unsuitable outputs, so input screening alone leaves a gap.

options.text: Screen incoming messages for signs of self-harm or abuse and route them to a human team
options.explanation: An input-side check is the right place to catch disclosures that need a person, not just a model reply.

options.text: Check each reply for unsuitable content before display, independently of input checks
options.explanation: An independent output check catches unsuitable replies however they arose, adding a second layer.

options.text: Put all safeguarding rules in the system prompt and drop the classifiers to cut latency
options.explanation: The system prompt is a soft layer, and removing independent checks leaves no defence if the model is steered.

options.text: Screen replies only after they are displayed so the output check never adds latency
options.explanation: A check that runs after display cannot stop unsuitable content from reaching the pupil.

explanation: Correct: B and C. Layered guardrails put independent checks on both sides of the model: input screening that routes safeguarding disclosures to people, and output screening that blocks unsuitable replies before display. Why not the others: A assumes clean inputs guarantee clean outputs; D collapses the layers into a single soft control; E runs the output check too late to prevent harm.

prompt: An accounts-payable agent has tools to read, send and delete email, update supplier bank details and issue payments. Fraudsters regularly impersonate suppliers to request bank-detail changes. Which TWO measures best reduce the risk from the agent's excessive agency? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Instruct the agent to be suspicious of bank-change emails and double-check before acting
options.explanation: A prompt instruction can be defeated by a convincing or injected email, so it cannot be the main control.

options.text: Drop the payment and delete tools triage does not need; route payments via human approval
options.explanation: Removing capabilities the task does not need shrinks what a manipulated agent can do.

options.text: Add a confidence parameter to each tool and reject calls the agent rates below a threshold
options.explanation: Self-declared confidence is easy for a manipulated agent to inflate and enforces nothing.

options.text: Hold bank-detail changes as pending until staff confirm them on a number already on file
options.explanation: An out-of-band check enforced outside the model stops fraudulent changes even if the agent is fooled.

options.text: Send every tool call to security monitoring for review at the weekly risk meeting
options.explanation: Monitoring helps detect abuse, but weekly review comes after the fraudulent payment has gone out.

explanation: Correct: B and D. Excessive agency is reduced by giving the agent only the tools its task needs and by enforcing high-risk actions outside the model, here an out-of-band verification the backend requires before a bank change takes effect. Why not the others: A and C rely on the agent's own judgement, which is exactly what the fraud targets; E is detective and too slow to prevent the loss.

prompt: An adviser-facing assistant answers questions over client portfolios through a query tool. Each adviser may see only their own clients. The team plans to enforce this with a system-prompt rule naming the clients each adviser may access. What should the architect change?

options.text: Keep the prompt rule but move it to the top of the system prompt and repeat it each turn
Keep the prompt rule and add an output filter that redacts any client name not in the list
Pass the adviser's identity to the query tool and enforce row-level access in the database
Give the tool read access to all portfolios but log every query for monthly access review

explanation: Correct: C. Authorisation belongs below the model: the tool runs with the adviser's identity and the data layer returns only rows that adviser may see, so a persuaded model cannot widen access. Why not the others: A relies on the model obeying text, which injection or error can defeat; B filters names after the data is fetched and misses other fields; D grants everything and only detects misuse afterwards.

prompt: A regional utility opens an engagement with "we want Claude to answer our customer emails" and the sponsor already has a vendor demo in mind. Before proposing any architecture, what should the architect do first?

options.text: Draft a proposal for an email-answering agent based on common patterns in the sector
Build a quick prototype on a sample of emails to show the sponsor what is possible today
Run structured discovery: who handles email today, how the process works, and what hurts
Ask which model the sponsor prefers so the design can be sized around that choice early

explanation: Correct: C. A request phrased as a solution needs discovery before design: who is affected, how the work is done today, where it fails, and how success will be measured; the email agent may or may not survive that. Why not the others: A commits to a solution before the problem is known; B anchors everyone on a prototype built on guesses; D asks an implementation question before the problem is known.

prompt: A product director tells the team to drop the retrieval step from a benefits-advice assistant to cut running cost by 40 percent. Evaluation shows the ungrounded version misstates policy figures far more often. What should the architect do?

options.text: Quantify the error increase and its consequences, recommend, and let the director decide
Comply with the instruction, since cost and scope decisions belong to the product director
Keep retrieval in place quietly and hide the cost in another line of the project budget
Escalate to the director's manager and ask for the instruction to be overruled on quality

explanation: Correct: A. A trade-off is communicated by putting the evidence (error rates, wrong advice to claimants, rework and complaints) next to the saving, making a clear recommendation, and leaving the accountable owner to decide with full information. Why not the others: B withholds a material risk from the decision-maker; C is deception that surfaces later; D escalates before the conversation with the owner has happened.

prompt: A sponsor wants a new ticket-triage assistant to resolve every support ticket with no human involvement from day one. Evaluation shows it handles routine categories well but fails on billing disputes and account security. Which approach best manages this?

options.text: Accept the full-automation target and plan to fix the weak categories after launch
Quietly take billing and security tickets out of scope so the headline target is met
Ignore the demand, since it is unrealistic and will be forgotten once the system ships
Show results by category, propose automating the strong ones, and agree a target rate

explanation: Correct: D. Expectation management rests on evidence: show where the assistant is reliable, propose automating those categories with human handling for the rest, and agree a measurable automation rate that can grow as evidence allows. Why not the others: A signs up to a target the evidence already contradicts; B changes scope behind the sponsor's back; C leaves the sponsor uninformed and the gap to surface at launch.

prompt: An innovation lab built a contract-summary assistant for a law firm's knowledge team, which will now own and run it. Beyond the source code, which set of artefacts matters most for a successful handoff?

options.text: The business case and the original statement of work that set out the engagement's scope
The chat transcripts the lab's engineers kept while using AI tools to build the system
A recording of the final demonstration and the slides shown to the firm's partners
Architecture docs with decision records, runbooks, the eval suite and a prompt guide

explanation: Correct: D. The receiving team must operate and evolve the system: decision records explain why it is built this way, runbooks how to run and recover it, the eval suite whether a change helped, and the prompt guide how to change behaviour safely. Why not the others: A describes what was agreed, not what was built; B is working history nobody will read; C is a snapshot of the journey, not a tool for ownership.

prompt: A procurement assistant has been live for a quarter. The steering committee receives a monthly dashboard of API calls, p95 latency and cache hit rate, and the sponsor is now questioning whether to renew funding. What change would most improve alignment?

options.text: Lead with the business outcomes agreed at discovery, with technical metrics as support
Send the dashboard every week instead of every month to keep the committee engaged
Add error budgets, token spend and uptime to the dashboard so that it looks more complete
Replace the written dashboard with a quarterly review meeting with the sponsor alone

explanation: Correct: A. The sponsor funded a business outcome, so reporting should lead with the success criteria agreed at discovery (cycle time, spend under contract) and use technical metrics as supporting evidence; that keeps the sponsorship feedback loop alive. Why not the others: B sends the wrong content more often; C deepens the mismatch with more technical detail; D reduces contact instead of fixing its content.

prompt: Which lifecycle phase does this activity belong to: shadowing a dispatch desk for a week to map how delivery exceptions are escalated today and where the handoffs between teams break down?

options.text: Design
Handoff
Monitoring
Discovery

explanation: Correct: D. Observing how the work is done today and where it fails is discovery, which establishes the problem before any solution is designed. Why not the others: A, design, would be choosing patterns and components against agreed requirements; B, handoff, is the transfer of a finished system to its operators; C, monitoring, is observing a system that is already in production.

prompt: An architect must explain to a non-technical steering committee why the team chose retrieval over fine-tuning for a policy assistant. Which way of communicating the decision is most effective?

options.text: Walk the committee through the embedding benchmarks and vector index settings in detail
State the decision only, since the committee does not need the technical reasoning
Frame it as speed of policy updates, cost and auditability, and record the trade-offs
Send the committee the technical design document and invite any questions by email

explanation: Correct: C. An architectural decision is communicated by translating it into the audience's terms (how fast policy changes take effect, cost, traceability) and leaving a written record of the options and trade-offs. Why not the others: A buries the committee in detail it cannot act on; B denies it the reasoning it needs to back the choice; D delegates the explanation to a document written for engineers.

prompt: A team is writing the architecture documentation for a Claude solution that other engineers will implement. Which content is most important to include so that implementation stays faithful to the design?

options.text: A pinned dependency manifest for the reference implementation the design team built
Components, data flows, prompts with owners, evaluation gates and decision rationale
A copy of the model provider's public documentation on the API and prompt engineering
A narrative of the project's history and the meetings where key decisions were taken

explanation: Correct: B. Implementation guidance needs the structure, the data flows (especially where sensitive data travels), the prompts as owned first-class artefacts, the quality gates a change must pass, and the rationale that stops implementers from undoing decisions. Why not the others: A is useful but says nothing about the design; C is already available to everyone; D is context, not guidance.

prompt: After four weeks of discovery for a freight broker's quoting assistant, the sponsor wants design to start on Monday. Which TWO outputs are the most important to have agreed in writing before design begins? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The final wording of the system prompt and few-shot examples the assistant will run with
The chosen vector store and the configuration it will run with in production
The sprint plan and staffing for the build phase that follows on from discovery
The problem statement with success criteria and how each criterion will be measured
The constraints: data sensitivity, compliance, integrations and non-functional targets

explanation: Correct: D and E. Discovery should close with an agreed problem and a measurable definition of success, plus the constraints the design must honour; without those, no design decision can be checked against anything. Why not the others: A is a build output; B is a design and implementation choice, premature at discovery; C is planning that follows from the design rather than an input to it.

prompt: During the build of a claims-triage assistant, the operations director asks almost weekly for another document type, a further team or a new language. Which TWO practices best manage this while keeping the relationship healthy? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Accept every request at once so the director stays engaged and supportive of the project
Refuse all changes until the original scope has shipped, then revisit the backlog
Log each request against the agreed scope and show its cost and risk before accepting it
Hold a regular prioritisation session where requests are traded off against commitments
Pad every estimate by 20 percent so new requests can be absorbed without any discussion

explanation: Correct: C and D. Scope is managed by making the impact of each change visible against the agreed baseline, and by giving stakeholders a structured forum in which they prioritise and trade off. Why not the others: A guarantees overrun with nothing visible until it is too late; B ignores legitimate change and damages the relationship; E hides the trade-off instead of surfacing it.

prompt: An assistant has been in production for six months. Which TWO activities belong to the monitoring and iteration phases of its lifecycle? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Interviewing stakeholders to decide whether the project should exist and what it solves
Tracking accuracy, latency, cost and safety against agreed targets and alerting on drift
Feeding reviewed production failures into the eval set and shipping gated prompt updates
Choosing between a workflow and an agent architecture for the core processing loop
Writing the first version of the runbook for the team that will take the system over

explanation: Correct: B and C. Monitoring watches live quality, latency, cost and safety and raises the alarm when they drift; iteration turns what monitoring and users find into evaluated, gated improvements. Why not the others: A is discovery, which decides whether and what to build; D is a design decision made before the build; E is handoff preparation, done before the operators take over.

prompt: An engagement has agreed its problem statement, success measures and constraints. Which TWO activities belong to the design phase that follows? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Choosing the retrieval strategy and deciding where guardrails and approvals sit
Observing how the finance team closes the books today and where effort is wasted
Selecting between a workflow and an agent for the core processing, with rationale
Transferring on-call duty and operating procedures to the client's support engineers
Using a quarter of production metrics to pick which failure modes to fix next

explanation: Correct: A and C. Design turns agreed requirements into architectural choices: the processing pattern, the retrieval approach and the control points, each with its rationale recorded. Why not the others: B is discovery, which has already closed; D is handoff, which comes after the build; E is monitoring and iteration, which follow launch.

prompt: A regional government agency wants an assistant that drafts benefit-eligibility letters for caseworkers. The request comes from the IT director, who holds the budget, and only IT staff attend the first discovery workshop. What should the architect do before agreeing the scope?

options.text: Treat the IT director's requirements as final, since IT funds and signs off the build
options.explanation: Funding the build does not make IT the owner of eligibility policy or of letter quality.

options.text: Find the owner of eligibility policy and letter sign-off, and interview the caseworkers
options.explanation: Right: the real decision-maker and the affected users must shape scope, and neither is in the room.

options.text: Build a quick prototype from sample letters so caseworkers can react once IT approves it
options.explanation: A prototype built on IT's assumptions anchors the design before the policy owner and users define it.

options.text: Survey all caseworkers for wanted features and rank the backlog by the number of votes
options.explanation: A feature vote skips the policy owner and collects wish lists rather than how the work is done.

explanation: Correct: B. Discovery has to identify who actually decides (here the owner of eligibility policy and letter quality) and the people whose work changes (the caseworkers). Why not the others: A confuses the budget holder with the authority for acceptance; C anchors on an unvalidated design before the right people are involved; D asks users for features instead of observing the work, and still omits the policy owner.

prompt: A logistics company wants Claude to classify inbound customs-exception emails and route them to the right desk. The sponsor says it will 'save the team a lot of time'. What should the architect do before building anything?

options.text: Measure today's volume, handling time per email, misrouting and rework rates as a baseline
options.explanation: Right: without a baseline of today's process there is no way to show or size the improvement.

options.text: Agree a 95 percent classification accuracy target and build the evaluation set around it
options.explanation: A target picked without knowing today's misrouting rate may be too lax or too strict.

options.text: Estimate token cost per email at expected volume so finance can approve the running budget
options.explanation: Cost matters, but it does not show whether the solution saves time against today's process.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to restate 'a lot of time' as a percentage and record it as the target
options.explanation: A percentage of an unmeasured quantity is still unmeasurable; the starting point comes first.

explanation: Correct: A. A vague benefit becomes testable only once the current process has been measured: volume, handling time, error and rework rates. The pilot can then be compared against that baseline. Why not the others: B sets a quality target without knowing the starting point; C is an input to the business case but says nothing about time; D records a percentage of a quantity nobody has measured.

prompt: Discovery for a hospital group's clinical-note summariser has captured the functional requirements in detail. Which additional information, if missed now, is most likely to force a redesign late in the project?

options.text: Each specialty's preferred summary length and tone, gathered from its senior clinicians
options.explanation: Useful for prompt tuning later, but style can be adjusted without changing the architecture.

options.text: A set of example notes that clinicians regard as the best summaries, to seed the eval set
options.explanation: Valuable for evaluation, but examples can be gathered later without redesigning the system.

options.text: Whether clinicians prefer bullet points or short prose for summaries read on the ward
options.explanation: An output-format preference is cheap to change and does not drive architectural choices.

options.text: Where patient data may be processed, how fast summaries are needed, and daily note volume
options.explanation: Right: residency, latency and volume constrain region, model choice and batch versus real-time design.

explanation: Correct: D. Non-functional requirements such as data residency, latency and volume decide the deployment region, the model and the processing pattern (real-time versus batch), so discovering them late means rework. Why not the others: A and C are presentation preferences that a prompt change can address; B helps build the evaluation set but can be collected at any point without changing the design.

prompt: A bank's proof of concept summarised 50 hand-picked loan files, and executives were impressed. They now want the assistant live for every branch next month. What is the architect's best recommendation?

options.text: Agree to the date, since feasibility is shown, and fix any issues through rapid hotfixes
options.explanation: Feasibility on curated files says little about real traffic, and fixing in production risks loan decisions.

options.text: Run a time-boxed pilot in a few branches on real files, with exit criteria agreed up front
options.explanation: Right: a pilot tests real conditions, and pre-agreed exit criteria turn go/no-go into evidence.

options.text: Extend the proof of concept with 500 more hand-picked files, then roll out to every branch
options.explanation: More curated files repeat the selection bias and still skip real users and workflows.

options.text: Ask the executives to wait until summaries of the original 50 files are flawless
options.explanation: Perfection on a small curated set is neither achievable nor evidence of real-world performance.

explanation: Correct: B. A proof of concept answers 'can it work?' on chosen inputs; a pilot answers 'does it work here?' on real traffic with real users, and exit criteria agreed up front (accuracy on unselected files, handling time, escalation rate) decide promotion. Why not the others: A skips that evidence entirely; C keeps the selection bias; D sets an absolute bar on the wrong data set.

prompt: An insurer must decide whether its claims assistant may email customers directly or only draft emails for staff to send. The architect is briefing the CISO, the general counsel and the COO separately. Which approach is most effective?

options.text: Show one deck with the full technical design and eval tables, identically to all three
options.explanation: Consistency matters, but an unfiltered technical deck buries the risks each audience must weigh.

options.text: Brief only the COO, since the executive makes the call and security and legal will follow
options.explanation: Security and legal hold veto-level concerns here; skipping them invites a late block.

options.text: Open every briefing with the model's public benchmark scores to persuade each audience
options.explanation: General benchmarks do not address this deployment's access, liability or cost questions.

options.text: Use the same facts and recommendation, but open each briefing with its audience's concern
options.explanation: Right: same facts, framed in the terms each audience uses to judge the trade-off.

explanation: Correct: D. Trade-offs are presented in each audience's terms without changing the facts: data flows, tool permissions and abuse paths for security; liability for customer-facing errors for legal; cost, throughput and residual risk for the COO. Why not the others: A is consistent but not tailored; B excludes stakeholders who can block the decision; C uses evidence that answers none of their questions.

prompt: A SaaS company chose a fixed-step workflow rather than an autonomous agent for customer onboarding. A year later, new engineers keep proposing a switch to an agent, and nobody remembers why it was rejected. Which artefact would best have prevented this?

options.text: A comment block in the orchestration module explaining how each step calls the model
options.explanation: Code comments explain how the code works, not which alternatives were rejected and why.

options.text: The slides from the original design review, stored on the shared drive by meeting date
options.explanation: Slides rarely record the reasoning, the consequences or when to revisit, and are hard to find.

options.text: A decision record with context, options weighed, the choice, consequences and triggers
options.explanation: Right: an ADR keeps the why, the rejected options and the conditions for reopening the decision.

options.text: A wiki page describing the current architecture with diagrams of each component
options.explanation: Describes what exists now, but not why the alternatives were rejected.

explanation: Correct: C. An architecture decision record captures the context, the options weighed, the choice, its consequences and the conditions that would justify revisiting it, so later teams can tell whether anything has changed. Why not the others: A documents the implementation, not the decision; B is an informal snapshot that usually lacks the rationale; D shows the current state but not why alternatives were rejected.

prompt: A media company is introducing Claude-generated article summaries. The editor-in-chief asks the architect directly: 'Will it make mistakes?' Which answer communicates the system's behaviour most responsibly?

options.text: Give the measured error rate on representative data, typical examples, and the controls
options.explanation: Right: an honest rate, what errors look like, and the controls around them.

options.text: Reassure the editor that the model is among the most capable and that mistakes are rare
options.explanation: Unquantified reassurance sets expectations the first visible error will break.

options.text: Explain how token sampling and temperature work so the editor understands why outputs vary
options.explanation: Accurate mechanics, but it does not say how often or how badly the system errs.

options.text: Explain that temperature zero makes output deterministic, so summaries will be error-free
options.explanation: Temperature zero does not make output fully deterministic, and consistency is not correctness.

explanation: Correct: A. Probabilistic behaviour is communicated as a measured rate on representative data, concrete examples of the failure types, the controls that catch them and how the rate is tracked after launch. Why not the others: B over-promises; C explains mechanisms without answering the question; D is wrong twice: temperature zero does not guarantee determinism, and consistency would not remove errors.

prompt: A retailer's contract for a staff-facing product assistant says 'responses within 2 seconds'. The vendor's dashboard shows the target met every month, yet store staff complain about slow answers. Which SLA definition would best resolve the dispute going forward?

options.text: Mean latency of model API calls taken from the vendor's logs, averaged over each month
options.explanation: Averages hide the slow tail, and the API misses retrieval, network and client time staff experience.

options.text: A percentile of end-to-end latency, measured where staff experience it, over a set window
options.explanation: Right: it pins down what is measured, where, at which percentile and over what period.

options.text: The maximum latency of any single request at the API gateway, with a penalty per breach
options.explanation: A strict maximum is dominated by outliers and still measures at the gateway, not where staff wait.

options.text: Uptime of the model endpoint, measured by synthetic health checks and reported each month
options.explanation: Availability is a separate objective and says nothing about how long staff wait.

explanation: Correct: B. A usable SLA states what is measured (end-to-end response, possibly time to first token too), where (the client side, as staff experience it), the statistic (a percentile such as p95 rather than a mean), the window and the exclusions. Why not the others: A uses a mean taken at the wrong point; C is measured at the wrong point and impractically strict; D measures availability, not latency.

prompt: A university's student-support assistant collects thumbs-up/down ratings and free-text comments. The feedback sits on a dashboard that nobody acts on. Which change would best turn it into improvement?

options.text: Triage negative feedback regularly, label causes, and add confirmed cases to the eval set
options.explanation: Right: it closes the loop so real failures become test cases that gate future changes.

options.text: Insert each thumbs-down conversation into the system prompt as an example of what to avoid
options.explanation: Unreviewed, ever-growing negative examples bloat the prompt and may teach the wrong lesson.

options.text: Report the monthly thumbs-up percentage to the sponsor as the primary quality metric
options.explanation: Satisfaction ratings are biased and coarse; reporting them does not identify or fix failures.

options.text: Remove the feedback buttons, since response rates are low and the signal is too noisy
options.explanation: Low volume is a reason to triage carefully, not to discard the only direct user signal.

explanation: Correct: A. User feedback becomes improvement when it is triaged, classified by root cause and converted into labelled test cases that the regression suite runs before every prompt or model change. Why not the others: B pushes raw, unreviewed data into the prompt; C turns a noisy proxy into the headline metric; D throws away a real signal instead of using it well.

prompt: A carrier piloted an assistant for delivery-exception handling with a target of 40 percent less handling time. The pilot achieved 12 percent, and one exception type performed poorly. The sponsor presents to the board next week. What should the architect do?

options.text: Report only the exception types that performed well, and give the overall figure later
options.explanation: Selective reporting misleads the board and damages trust when the full figure surfaces.

options.text: Re-run the measurement without the weak exception type so the headline nears the target
options.explanation: Changing the population after the fact to hit a target is misrepresentation, not analysis.

options.text: Report the result against target by exception type with causes, and set out costed options
options.explanation: Right: honest results plus a diagnosis and costed options let the sponsor decide informed.

options.text: Recommend going to production, since 12 percent is positive, and raise the shortfall later
options.explanation: Skipping the shortfall hides a material gap and scales a partly failing design.

explanation: Correct: C. A disappointing pilot is reported as it is, with a breakdown showing where value was and was not delivered, the causes found, and costed options (narrow scope to the types that work, fix the weak type, or stop) plus a recommendation. Why not the others: A hides part of the evidence; B changes the population to flatter the result; D avoids the conversation and scales a partly failing design.

prompt: An education-technology company's essay-feedback assistant is pinned to a specific model version. The provider has announced that version's deprecation with a retirement date several months away. Which TWO actions should the architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Switch production to the provider's newest model alias on the day of the announcement
options.explanation: An unevaluated switch can change feedback quality and format for students without warning.

options.text: Keep the pinned version until retirement and start migration only once calls begin to fail
options.explanation: Waiting for failures turns a planned change into an outage with no time to evaluate.

options.text: Run the eval suite on candidate replacements and adjust prompts where behaviour differs
options.explanation: Right: the eval suite provides evidence for choosing and tuning the replacement.

options.text: Change the model silently and ask teachers to report any differences they happen to notice
options.explanation: Relying on ad hoc user reports replaces evaluation with chance and erodes trust.

options.text: Agree a dated migration plan with owners, staged rollout, user communication and rollback
options.explanation: Right: a dated, owned plan with staged rollout and rollback manages the change before the deadline.

explanation: Correct: C and E. Model retirement is a planned lifecycle event: re-run the evaluation suite on candidate replacements to see how quality, latency and cost change and where prompts need adjusting, then run an owned, dated migration with staged rollout, user communication and rollback. Why not the others: A switches without evidence; B waits for an outage; D treats users as the test harness.

prompt: An operations team is taking over an invoice-extraction pipeline built on Claude. The architect is writing the runbook they will use on call. Which TWO items belong in the runbook? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The history of prompt iterations during design, with why each earlier version was rejected
options.explanation: Useful design history for an ADR or changelog, not what on-call staff need in an incident.

options.text: Symptom-to-action steps for known failures such as rate limits or malformed-output spikes
options.explanation: Right: on-call staff need to recognise a failure quickly and know the first steps to take.

options.text: The full rationale for the evaluation methodology, with sample sizes and scoring rubrics
options.explanation: Belongs in the evaluation documentation; it does not help someone respond to an incident.

options.text: A summary of the model's capabilities and the vendor's roadmap of upcoming releases
options.explanation: Background reading that does not help diagnose or recover from an operational problem.

options.text: Escalation contacts, how to pause automation for manual handling, and how to roll back
options.explanation: Right: safe degradation, rollback and escalation are core runbook content.

explanation: Correct: B and E. A runbook is operational: how to recognise known failure modes and confirm them on the dashboards, and how to contain, degrade safely, roll back and escalate. Why not the others: A is decision history that belongs in ADRs or a changelog; C belongs in the evaluation documentation; D is general background that helps nobody act during an incident.

prompt: A pharmaceutical company's regulatory-document assistant is moving from a vendor build team to an internal platform team and the regulatory affairs unit. Which TWO arrangements most reduce the risk of ownership gaps after handoff? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Keep the vendor's lead architect as accountable owner for the whole system indefinitely
options.explanation: This leaves accountability outside the organisation that runs and answers for the system.

options.text: Name a single accountable owner per area (prompts, incidents, cost, data access) in a RACI
options.explanation: Right: a RACI with one accountable owner per area removes ambiguity about who decides and acts.

options.text: Give regulatory affairs the quality decisions, and the platform team uptime and deployment
options.explanation: Right: domain experts own what good means, while engineers own how it runs.

options.text: Make the whole platform team jointly accountable for every area so anyone can act
options.explanation: Shared accountability for everything usually means nobody is accountable for anything.
