options.text: Postpone ownership decisions until the first production incident shows where the gaps are
options.explanation: Learning ownership from an incident in a regulated setting finds the gap at the worst time.

explanation: Correct: B and C. Handoff needs explicit ownership: a RACI with exactly one accountable owner per operational area, and a split that puts quality judgements with the domain owners and runtime operation with the platform team. Why not the others: A leaves accountability outside the organisation; D spreads it so thinly that nobody holds it; E finds the gaps through an incident, which is costly in a regulated domain.

prompt: At a fintech, a well-meant prompt edit made directly in production caused the support assistant to quote an outdated fee schedule for two days. Which TWO controls should the architect introduce? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Restrict prompt editing to the most senior engineer, so changes are rare and well informed
options.explanation: Fewer editors reduces volume but still lets untested changes reach production.

options.text: Version prompts with peer review, deploy them through the pipeline, and trace the version
options.explanation: Right: versioned, reviewed and traceable prompts make changes auditable and attributable.

options.text: Freeze the prompt after launch and route every improvement into the next major release
options.explanation: A permanent freeze blocks urgent fixes and pushes teams back toward unofficial edits.

options.text: Gate each prompt change on the regression eval suite, then stage the rollout with rollback
options.explanation: Right: eval gates catch regressions, and staged rollout with rollback limits the damage.

options.text: Ask editors to record each change in a shared spreadsheet after making it in production
options.explanation: An after-the-fact log documents changes but prevents nothing and is easily skipped.

explanation: Correct: B and D. Prompts are production configuration and need the same change control as code: versioning, review, pipeline deployment and traceability, plus regression evaluation gates, staged rollout and rollback. Why not the others: A narrows who can edit without adding any testing; C blocks legitimate fixes; E records changes after the fact and prevents nothing.

prompt: A retailer launched a returns-handling assistant two weeks ago. The sponsor's funding review is in a month, but the agreed success measure, hours saved per month, needs a full quarter of data. The sponsor asks what to show. What should the architect propose?

options.text: Present the pilot's accuracy scores from the eval suite as the measure of value delivered
Report adoption and deflection indicators now, with hours saved as the later measure
Ask the sponsor to postpone the funding review until the quarter of data exists
Extrapolate the first two weeks of usage to a full quarter and present the projection

explanation: Correct: B. Lagging outcomes such as hours saved take time to accumulate, so the review should see leading indicators that predict them (adoption, share of returns handled without staff, user ratings), with the business measure reported once the data exists. Why not the others: A reports a technical quality score, not value; C leaves the sponsor with nothing to defend the budget; D presents a guess as a result.

prompt: An insurer wants a four-week proof of concept for a claims-letter assistant. The sponsor asks for single sign-on, full claims-system integration and a polished interface in that window. What should the architect propose the proof of concept sets out to prove?

options.text: Whether the model drafts acceptable letters from real claim data, with all else stubbed
Whether the full production integration can be delivered inside the four-week window
Whether the chosen interface design satisfies claims handlers before any model work starts
Whether single sign-on and access control work with the insurer's identity provider

explanation: Correct: A. A proof of concept exists to retire the riskiest assumption, here whether the model can produce acceptable letters from real data; integration, identity and polish are solved problems for the pilot and build. Why not the others: B spends the window on plumbing, not on the open question; C judges presentation before there is anything to show; D tests infrastructure the insurer already knows how to build.

prompt: A fintech's platform group has 60 engineers using Claude Code in one monorepo. Each engineer wrote their own setup notes, so sessions use different test commands and style rules, and onboarding a newcomer takes days. What is the most effective enablement step?

options.text: Publish a wiki page of recommended settings and ask every engineer to apply it by hand
Pair each newcomer with an early adopter who shares their personal setup
Limit the tool to a small guild of experts until conventions settle
Commit a project instructions file and permission settings to the repository

explanation: Correct: D. Configuration every session needs belongs in the repository: a committed instructions file carries conventions and commands, and project settings carry permissions, so every session starts from one reviewed baseline. Why not the others: A relies on people remembering to apply a page; B spreads one person's habits rather than a team standard; C delays adoption and yields no shared configuration.

prompt: An insurer's engineers ask the Claude Code session that just implemented a feature to review its own diff before opening a pull request. The self-reviews approve almost everything, and regressions are rising. Which adjustment most directly improves review quality?

options.text: Review the diff in a fresh session with explicit criteria and a human owning the merge
Instruct the same session to be far stricter and to list five problems before it approves
Drop AI review and rely on the existing test suite to catch regressions
Relax the merge bar so fixes for regressions can ship faster when they appear

explanation: Correct: A. A reviewer that shares the author's context inherits the author's assumptions and blind spots; a fresh session judging the diff against stated criteria restores an independent check, and a human still decides the merge. Why not the others: B manufactures findings inside the same anchored context; C removes a useful check instead of fixing how it is run; D ships defects faster rather than catching them.

prompt: A travel company's booking agent has, since yesterday, cancelled a handful of reservations that customers only asked to modify. The on-call engineer proposes rewriting the system prompt tonight. What should happen first?

options.text: Rewrite the system prompt now, since prompt wording is the usual cause
Pull the traces for the affected sessions and contain the blast radius
Roll back to the previous model version before looking any further
Take the agent offline for good and rebuild it with stricter controls

explanation: Correct: B. Evidence comes before treatment: the traces show what the agent actually saw and did, which separates a prompt problem from injected content, a bad tool result or a data change, while containment such as disabling the cancel action limits harm meanwhile. Why not the others: A changes the system before the cause is known; C guesses at a different cause; D is disproportionate for a handful of requests.

prompt: A team wants AI-assisted coding to speed up routine work without letting unreviewed changes reach the main branch. Which workflow change achieves this?

options.text: Let the assistant push straight to the main branch so it never has to wait on a reviewer
Run the assistant only in a sandbox with no access to the repository
Let the assistant open branches and pull requests that need CI and a human review
Have a human retype every suggested line so nothing is committed unread

explanation: Correct: C. The assistant stays inside the existing safety net: it works on branches, its pull requests run the automated checks, and a human decides the merge, so routine work speeds up without anything unreviewed reaching main. Why not the others: A removes the review gate entirely; B removes the access the assistant needs to be useful; D removes the speed the team wanted in the first place.

prompt: An engineer debugging a failing Claude integration sees the model returning malformed JSON in roughly one response in fifty. Which approach resolves this most robustly?

options.text: Add "please return valid JSON" to the prompt and check that the next few replies parse
Constrain output to a schema such as a tool definition, validate in code, and retry
Use a lenient parser and silently skip any response that still fails to parse
Rotate to a different model whenever a malformed response is observed

explanation: Correct: B. Reliable structured output comes from constraining the response to a schema, validating it in code, and defining what happens on the rare miss, such as a retry or a fallback. Why not the others: A lowers the rate but leaves the failure unhandled when it recurs; C drops data silently and hides the problem; D adds variability without adding any handling of bad output.

prompt: A manufacturing group's platform team is extending Claude Code from two pilot squads to forty teams. Leadership wants the speed the pilots showed, but with no increase in operational risk. Which TWO practices best support this? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Versioned baseline project configuration and permission settings for teams to adopt
The same CI checks and review rules for AI-authored changes as for human ones
Letting each team grant whatever permission the assistant happens to request mid-session
Turning off logging of assistant actions to protect developer privacy
Allowing the assistant to deploy to production once the test suite is green

explanation: Correct: A and B. Scaling safely needs a shared starting point and no exemptions: a versioned baseline spreads proven configuration to every team, and holding AI-authored changes to the same checks and review keeps the existing quality gates intact. Why not the others: C lets permissions sprawl with no review; D removes the visibility needed to operate the tooling; E bypasses the human gate before production.

prompt: A bank is rolling Claude Code out to 300 engineers across dozens of repositories. The security team requires that no session, in any repository, can read files under the secrets and credentials paths, and that neither a repository's configuration nor an individual engineer can loosen this. Which configuration meets the requirement?

options.text: An organisation-wide CLAUDE.md pushed to every laptop that forbids opening those files
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md is guidance the model reads; the client does not enforce it.

options.text: A deny rule for those paths in each repository's committed `.claude/settings.json`
options.explanation: Works only where someone added it, and repository maintainers can edit or remove it.

options.text: A deny rule for those paths in every engineer's user settings, applied at onboarding
options.explanation: User settings belong to the engineer, who can change or delete the rule.

options.text: Deny rules for those paths in the managed settings that IT delivers to every machine
options.explanation: Managed settings take precedence, and a deny cannot be re-allowed at another scope.

explanation: Correct: D. Managed settings are delivered centrally, outrank user, project and local files, and a deny rule holds regardless of allow rules elsewhere, so no repository or engineer can reopen those paths. Why not the others: A is guidance the model reads, not a control the client enforces; B needs every repository to carry the rule and lets maintainers remove it; C lives in a file each engineer can edit.

prompt: A retail engineering team's CLAUDE.md says "run the formatter and linter after editing any file". Claude Code follows it most of the time, but roughly one pull request in ten still fails CI on formatting. The team wants formatting to happen after every edit without depending on the model remembering. What should they configure?

options.text: Rewrite the CLAUDE.md line in capitals as IMPORTANT and repeat it at the top and bottom
options.explanation: Stronger wording raises compliance, but the model can still skip an instruction.

options.text: A post-edit hook in committed project settings that runs the formatter and linter
options.explanation: The client runs hooks on the matching event, so formatting happens every time.

options.text: A formatting subagent that the main session is told to delegate to after editing
options.explanation: Delegation is still a model decision and can be skipped like the instruction.

options.text: A custom slash command that formats and lints, which developers run before each commit
options.explanation: This moves the reliance from the model's memory to the developer's memory.

explanation: Correct: B. A PostToolUse hook on edit and write tools is run by Claude Code itself after each successful edit, turning a request the model usually honours into a guaranteed step, and committing it gives every teammate the same behaviour. Why not the others: A only strengthens a suggestion the model may skip; C still depends on the model choosing to delegate; D swaps model forgetfulness for human forgetfulness.

prompt: A health-tech team uses Claude Code for a large refactor. Midway, they want an independent check of every changed module against their data-handling rules. The check reads hundreds of files and would flood the main session's context, and the reviewer must not be able to modify code. Which setup fits best?

options.text: Fork the current conversation and instruct the fork not to edit anything it reviews
options.explanation: A fork inherits the full conversation and tool pool; read-only rests on an instruction.

options.text: Add a CLAUDE.md rule that reviews are read-only, then review in the main session
options.explanation: Review output fills the main context, and read-only depends on the model obeying.

options.text: Review in the main session and compact whenever the context fills up
options.explanation: Compaction loses detail mid-review and the main session keeps its edit tools.

options.text: A project subagent with a reviewer prompt and only read and search tools
options.explanation: Subagents get their own context and a tools list that can exclude edit tools.

explanation: Correct: D. A subagent runs in its own context, so the file reads stay out of the main session and only findings return; its tools list can omit edit tools, and a fresh context is not anchored on the author's reasoning. Why not the others: A inherits the whole conversation and every tool; B and C keep the noise in the main context and rely on instructions rather than tool access to stay read-only.

prompt: A logistics company has an internal MCP server for its shipment-tracking API. The 25 developers on the routing team each add it by hand, and its address and options have drifted between machines. Each developer holds a personal API key, and no credential may be committed. What should they do?

options.text: Publish the setup command on the wiki for each developer to re-add in user scope
options.explanation: Per-person configuration caused the drift; a wiki page keeps nothing in sync.

options.text: Commit a project `.mcp.json` that embeds one shared service-account key used by all clones
options.explanation: This commits a credential and replaces personal keys with one shared identity.

options.text: Commit a project `.mcp.json` that reads each developer's key from an environment variable
options.explanation: Project scope shares one versioned definition; expansion keeps keys out of the repo.

options.text: Describe the API's endpoints in CLAUDE.md so Claude calls them with shell commands
options.explanation: This abandons typed MCP tools, and the key still has to be supplied on each call.

explanation: Correct: C. A project-scoped `.mcp.json` is meant to be committed so everyone gets the same server definition, and Claude Code expands environment variable references in it, so each developer's key comes from their shell rather than the file. Why not the others: A preserves the drift; B commits a secret and loses per-user attribution; D drops MCP and still needs the key supplied on every call.

prompt: A SaaS company's support agent gave a customer a wrong refund amount. The customer's ticket includes the request id. An engineer pastes the same question into a playground with the current prompt and gets a correct answer, so they propose closing the ticket as not reproducible. What should the engineer do instead?

options.text: Pull the trace for the request id, replay its exact inputs offline, and keep it as a test
options.explanation: The trace holds the real prompt version, context and tool outputs, so replay reproduces it.

options.text: Rerun the question in the playground at higher temperature until the wrong amount appears
options.explanation: Sampling a different context may never hit a cause that lay in retrieved data or tools.

options.text: Roll the production prompt back at once, since the error followed the latest deployment
options.explanation: Acting on timing alone may revert a good change and leave the actual fault in place.

options.text: Tell the agent in the system prompt to double-check refunds and watch for complaints
options.explanation: This guesses at a fix and offers no way to confirm the original failure is resolved.

explanation: Correct: A. The playground differs from production in what usually causes such errors: prompt version, retrieved documents, tool results and parameters. The request id yields the full trace, so the engineer can replay it, find the faulty step and keep it as a regression case. Why not the others: B samples a different context; C acts on correlation, not evidence; D changes behaviour blind and cannot verify the fix.

prompt: A university's platform team wants Claude Code to run in its nightly CI pipeline: read the failing test logs, explain the likely causes, and feed a structured summary into a dashboard. No one is present during the run. Which setup is most appropriate?

options.text: Drive an interactive session in a terminal multiplexer and have the job type the request
options.explanation: Scripting an interactive session is brittle, and a permission prompt would stall the run.

options.text: Run the job with every permission check bypassed so it never stops to ask overnight
options.explanation: Bypassing all checks gives an unattended job far more power than reading logs needs.

options.text: Scrape the plain terminal output of a normal run and pull fields out with regexes
options.explanation: Parsing free-form console text breaks whenever the wording changes.

options.text: Use non-interactive mode with JSON output and a narrow list of pre-approved tools
options.explanation: Headless mode suits CI, JSON output is machine-readable, and an allowlist keeps it least-privileged.

explanation: Correct: D. Non-interactive print mode runs a prompt to completion without a terminal UI, can return JSON for the pipeline to parse, and lets the job pre-approve only the tools it needs, so it neither stalls on a prompt nor gains broad power. Why not the others: A drives an interactive session that can hang waiting for approval; B strips the guardrails from an unattended job; C parses fragile text meant for humans.

prompt: An open-source project runs Claude Code non-interactively in CI on each external pull request's checkout to draft a review. A security engineer warns that a malicious pull request could add hooks or an MCP server to the checkout's Claude Code settings, which CI would then execute. Which TWO measures address this risk? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run in a mode that loads no hooks, MCP servers or CLAUDE.md from the repository checkout
options.explanation: If the run never loads repository-supplied hooks or servers, a PR cannot inject code through them.

options.text: Use an isolated runner with no deployment secrets and a token that only posts comments
options.explanation: Least privilege limits the damage if anything untrusted does execute.

options.text: Rely on the workspace trust prompt that asks before repository hooks or MCP servers run
options.explanation: A non-interactive run shows no trust dialog or approval prompt, so this does not apply in CI.

options.text: Add a CLAUDE.md line telling Claude to ignore configuration introduced by a pull request
options.explanation: Hooks and MCP servers are run by the client, not the model, and the PR can edit CLAUDE.md too.

options.text: Add deny rules for dangerous commands to `.claude/settings.json` in the PR's checkout
options.explanation: The attacker controls that checkout and can change or remove the file.

explanation: Correct: A and B. The risk is executing untrusted configuration: A removes the injection path by never loading repository hooks, MCP servers or CLAUDE.md, and B limits the blast radius with an isolated, secret-free runner and a minimal token. Why not the others: C fails because headless runs show no trust or approval prompts; D relies on the model for what the client executes; E trusts a file the attacker controls.

prompt: A marketplace runs three Claude-backed features behind one API key. Finance reports that monthly spend has doubled, but engineering cannot say which feature, prompt version or model drove the increase. Which change gives the team what it needs?

options.text: Tag each request with feature, prompt version and model, and log its token usage per call
Move all traffic to a smaller model until spend returns to last month's level
Lower the maximum output tokens on every call so no single response is expensive
Ask each feature owner to estimate their share of spend and reconcile it with the invoice

explanation: Correct: A. Cost attribution needs per-request telemetry: when every call carries its feature, prompt version and model and records its token counts, spend can be broken down and the increase traced to one change. Why not the others: B treats the symptom and may degrade quality without locating the cost; C caps responses blindly and can truncate useful output; D produces guesses rather than measurements.
